label: Chess
card: Chess ends in checkmate when the opposing king is attacked and no legal move can remove the threat. The king is never actually captured. A different ending, stalemate, occurs when a player has no legal move but their king is not attacked.
claim_review: Articles 1.4 and 5.2.1 support the objective, prohibition of king capture and contrasting stalemate condition; no claim that every immobile king is stalemated.
relation_note: The laws distinguish checkmate from stalemate through whether the immobile side's king is attacked.
relation_locator: Articles 1.4 and 5.2.1

label: Go
card: Go players place stones on grid intersections to surround space. Connected stones share liberties: empty neighboring intersections along the grid lines. When an opponent occupies every liberty, the whole connected string is captured, linking local fights over stones with the larger struggle for territory.
claim_review: BGA introduction and capture paragraphs support intersections, orthogonal liberties and capture of a connected string; diagonal contact is not treated as connection.
relation_note: The teaching guide explains Go capture through the shared liberties of connected stones.
relation_locator: Introduction; Capturing stones and counting liberties

label: Shogi
card: Shogi is Japanese chess with a distinctive form of piece reuse. Captured pieces become reserves for their captor. Instead of moving a piece already on the board, a player can spend a turn returning a captured piece to play on their own side.
claim_review: Player's Guide PDF pages 1, 3 and 12 directly support Japanese chess, capture reserves and replacing a board move with a drop; omit its overbroad placement and promotion claims.
relation_note: The guide explicitly compares shogi with European chess and identifies returning captured pieces as a difference.
relation_locator: PDF page 3, Comparisons and Unique features of Shogi

label: Backgammon
card: Backgammon combines a race with obstacles. Each player moves fifteen checkers according to dice rolls, aiming to gather them in the home board and remove them. Landing on a lone opposing checker sends it to the bar, where it must re-enter before other checkers move.
claim_review: USBGF Object, Movement and Hitting sections support fifteen checkers, dice movement, bearing-off objective and priority of bar entry; a hit requires landing on a lone checker.
relation_note: The rules make re-entry of hit checkers a compulsory interruption of normal checker movement.
relation_locator: Hitting and Entering

label: Othello
card: Othello changes the ownership of pieces already on the board. A player places a disc to bracket an uninterrupted line of opposing discs, then flips those discs to their color. The winner has more discs when neither player can make a legal move.
claim_review: Official outflanking and ending rules support placement, flipping and the final majority; the game need not fill all sixty-four squares.
relation_note: A lack of outflanking moves determines both forced passes and the eventual end of the game.
relation_locator: Rules 2 and 8

label: Contract bridge
card: In contract bridge, four players form two partnerships. Bidding establishes a contract specifying a number of tricks and a trump suit, or no trumps. During play, one partner's cards are exposed as dummy, and the declarer chooses cards from both partnership hands.
claim_review: ACBL Basics, Auction and Play support partnerships, contract denomination and dummy control; bidding numbers count tricks above the initial six, so the card avoids equating the printed bid with total tricks.
relation_note: ACBL's play explanation assigns the exposed partnership hand to declarer's decisions after the auction.
relation_locator: Play: declaring side, declarer and dummy

label: Senet
card: Senet used a thirty-square board in ancient Egypt. Its imagery became more than decoration: during the New Kingdom, the game's passage through marked hazards was associated with the deceased person's journey toward the afterlife. Surviving game boxes connect recreation with funerary belief.
claim_review: The Met's Senet and importance sections support thirty squares, New Kingdom association and funerary objects; avoid presenting reconstructed detailed rules as certain.
relation_note: The museum documents double-sided game boxes carrying senet on one side and Twenty Squares on the other.
relation_locator: Opening paragraph and the two game sections

label: Twenty Squares
card: Twenty Squares spread across the ancient Near East and was later imported into Egypt. Surviving boards reveal adaptation rather than simple copying: special squares on Near Eastern examples display rosettes, while Egyptian examples use hieroglyphs. A shared game could acquire a different visual language.
claim_review: The Met explicitly reports geographic spread, import into Egypt and contrasting markings; no claim that all surviving boards preserve markings or identical rules.
relation_note: The museum describes Egyptian boxes accommodating both games, making their material comparison explicit.
relation_locator: Opening paragraph; Twenty Squares, Why is this game important?

label: Dick Fosbury
card: Dick Fosbury's lasting influence came from the high-jump technique bearing his name. He won Olympic gold in 1968, but his legacy extended beyond that result: the Fosbury Flop transformed how the event was approached. Olympedia distinguishes this technical influence from his relatively brief competitive prominence.
claim_review: Olympedia biography supports 1968 gold, technique and enduring influence; the card does not invent biomechanical details absent from this source.
relation_note: The biography identifies Fosbury's innovation and Olympic result specifically with the high-jump event.
relation_locator: Biographical paragraph and Olympic results

label: James Naismith
card: James Naismith devised basketball at Springfield in 1891 to provide an engaging indoor winter activity. Avoiding the rough collisions of outdoor games shaped the design. Elevated peach baskets required players to toss the ball toward a goal rather than charge through it.
claim_review: Springfield's account supports the winter brief, concern about roughness, elevated baskets and tossing; it does not establish that every modern rule originated unchanged in 1891.
relation_note: The college's historical account identifies Naismith as basketball's inventor and explains the game's design constraints.
relation_locator: A New Game; The Birth of Basketball

label: En passant
card: An en passant capture answers a pawn's two-square first advance. An opposing pawn beside its destination may capture it as though it had moved only one square. The opportunity exists only on the immediately following move; waiting forfeits this particular capture.
claim_review: FIDE 3.7.3.1–2 supports neighboring same-rank pawns, the two-square advance and immediate-next-move limit; no other capture window is implied.
relation_note: FIDE defines en passant as a special pawn capture within the chess movement rules.

label: Castling
card: Castling moves a king and rook in one turn, but permission depends on more than empty squares. Moving the king or the relevant rook permanently loses that castling right. Pieces between them or attacks on the king's starting, crossing or destination square can temporarily prevent it.
claim_review: FIDE 3.8.2 distinguishes forfeited rights from temporary obstruction; the attacked-square restriction concerns the king's route, not every square the rook crosses.
relation_note: FIDE explicitly defines castling as a king-and-rook move within the chess movement rules.
relation_locator: Article 3.8.2

label: Stalemate
card: Stalemate is a drawn chess position in which the player to move has no legal move and their king is not in check. The distinction from checkmate is crucial: immobilizing the opponent does not win if no attack on the king accompanies that immobilization.
claim_review: FIDE 5.2.1 supports side-to-move, absence of any legal move, no check and immediate draw; immobility of one piece alone is insufficient.
relation_note: The laws define stalemate as one of chess's game-ending draw conditions.
relation_locator: Article 5.2.1

label: Dead position in chess
card: A dead position ends a chess game because neither player could checkmate through any possible sequence of legal moves. This is stronger than saying that checkmate seems unlikely or cannot be forced: even cooperative play by the opponent would not make mate possible.
claim_review: FIDE 5.2.2 quantifies over any legal sequence; the cooperative-play explanation unpacks that condition rather than adding a material-count rule.
relation_note: Both end the game as a draw, but stalemate concerns present legal moves while dead position concerns impossibility of future mate.
relation_locator: Articles 5.2.1–5.2.2

label: Touch-move rule
card: In over-the-board chess, deliberately touching one of your pieces with the intention of moving it normally commits you to move that piece if a legal move exists. Adjusting a piece after announcing that intention is different. Accidental contact is not treated as deliberate selection.
claim_review: FIDE 4.2–4.5 support intentional contact, prior adjustment declaration and legal-move qualification; this describes own-piece handling rather than every multi-piece exception.
relation_note: FIDE's Act of Moving the Pieces regulates how a player's physical selection becomes binding.
relation_locator: Articles 4.2–4.5

label: Threefold repetition
card: Under the cited FIDE rules, threefold repetition creates a claimable draw rather than automatically stopping play. A player whose turn it is may claim when the position has just appeared for the third time, or first record an intended move that will produce that recurrence.
claim_review: FIDE 9.2.1–2 supports both current-position and intended-move claims by the player to move; the contrast with 9.6.1 avoids repeating only fivefold's position-identity lesson.
relation_note: The rules distinguish a player's threefold claim from the automatic fivefold repetition draw.
relation_locator: Articles 9.2 and 9.6.1

label: Underpromotion
card: A pawn reaching its final rank need not become a queen. Underpromotion chooses a rook, bishop or knight instead. The new piece takes effect immediately, and the available choices do not depend on which pieces were captured earlier in the game.
claim_review: FIDE 3.7.3.3–5 support all alternatives, immediate effect and independence from captured pieces; no unsupported tactical claim explains why a particular choice wins.
relation_note: FIDE's pawn-promotion rule explicitly permits the three non-queen choices described here.

label: Liberties in Go
card: A liberty is an empty intersection directly beside a Go stone along a horizontal or vertical line. Connected stones share their liberties as one string. Surrounding every liberty captures the entire string, so adding a connection can change the survival prospects of several stones at once.
claim_review: BGA capture section supports orthogonal adjacency and whole-string treatment; the connection consequence follows directly from sharing the resulting string's liberties.
relation_note: The Go guide uses liberties to define when individual stones and connected strings are captured.
relation_locator: Capturing stones and counting liberties

label: Eyes in Go
card: An eye is an internal space in a connected Go group. Two genuine, separate eyes can keep a group safe: an opponent cannot fill both in one move, and occupying the first would be self-capture rather than capturing the surrounding stones.
claim_review: BGA Life and death and self-capture examples support two-eye safety; genuine eyes prevents confusing superficial holes with the protected spaces in the rule explanation.
relation_note: The guide explains eye-based survival through internal liberties and the prohibition on noncapturing self-capture.
relation_locator: Self-capture examples; Life and death and the concept of eyes

label: Ko rule
card: A ko capture can create an opportunity for immediate recapture that would restore the previous position. The basic ko rule forbids that immediate reply. The player must first play elsewhere, giving the opponent an opportunity to respond or end the local cycle.
claim_review: BGA ko diagrams and explanatory paragraph support immediate-recapture restriction and intervening play; this does not claim that a single intervening move overrides every superko rule.
relation_note: Immediate ko and situational superko both limit repetition, but the latter also addresses longer cycles such as triple ko.
relation_locator: BGA How to Play, The ko rule; BGA Default Rules, Triple Ko

label: Seki
card: Seki is mutual survival in Go without each group having two independent eyes. Neighboring groups share a shortage of liberties, and either player's attempt to capture can allow the opponent to capture first. Leaving the position alone therefore preserves both sides' stones.
claim_review: BGA's seki examples support mutual stand-off and shortage of liberties; no universal territory-scoring rule is added because rulesets differ.
relation_note: The guide introduces seki as an exception to the simple expectation that a group lacking two eyes will die.
relation_locator: Seki: a kind of local stalemate

label: Komi
card: Komi compensates the player using White stones for Black's first move in Go. It adds points to White's final score rather than adding stones to the board. The British Go Association's cited default uses seven-and-a-half points; other rules or agreements can use different values.
claim_review: BGA Default Rules gives 7½ and contrasts traditional Japanese values; How to Play explains compensation rather than placement of stones.
relation_note: The tournament rules identify komi as a score adjustment within Go, separately from handicap-stone placement.
relation_locator: Default Rules, Komi; How to Play, Komi

label: Situational superko
card: Under the British Go Association's AGA-style rule, a player cannot make a play that recreates a board position previously created by that player. This reaches beyond immediate ko recapture, preventing longer repeating cycles such as triple ko from continuing indefinitely.
claim_review: The precise BGA same-player formulation and triple-ko motivation are retained; this is not asserted to describe every international superko variant.
relation_note: BGA describes its superko restriction as preventing triple ko and other repeated positions beyond the basic local cycle.
relation_locator: Default Rules, Triple Ko

label: Area and territory scoring in Go
card: Territory scoring counts enclosed empty points and captured stones; area scoring counts enclosed points and stones still occupying the board. That difference changes whether filling your own territory costs a point. AGA rules use pass stones to permit territory-style counting within an area-scoring framework.
claim_review: BGA comparison explicitly supports both definitions, defensive-fill consequence and pass-stone accommodation; the card avoids claiming universal exact equality of final counts.
relation_note: The comparison identifies these as alternative Go scoring systems and explains their practical counting differences.
relation_locator: Scoring; Does it cost me a point to make a defensive move inside my territory?

label: Doubling cube
card: Backgammon's doubling cube lets a player offer to raise the game's value before rolling. The opponent can decline and concede at the old value, or accept. Acceptance transfers ownership of the cube, so only that player may offer the next redouble.
claim_review: USBGF Doubling supports timing, decline cost and ownership transfer; describe points rather than instructing anyone to gamble or implying tournament exceptions do not exist.
relation_note: The federation presents the cube as the game's mechanism for offering and accepting increased stakes.
relation_locator: Doubling

label: Gammon
card: A backgammon loser who has not removed any checkers suffers a gammon, worth twice the doubling cube's value under standard scoring. If that loser also has a checker on the bar or in the winner's home board, the loss is instead a triple-value backgammon.
claim_review: USBGF Gammons and Backgammons supports the two scoring conditions; standard scoring qualification leaves room for the separately selected optional Jacoby rule.
relation_note: USBGF explicitly describes Jacoby as an optional rule changing when gammon and backgammon multipliers count.
relation_locator: Gammons and Backgammons; Optional Rules

label: Bearing off in backgammon
card: Bearing off removes checkers from a backgammon board, but only after all your active checkers reach your home board. A roll normally removes a checker from its matching point. An oversized roll can remove the highest remaining checker when no checker occupies a higher point.
claim_review: USBGF Bearing Off supplies prerequisites and oversized-roll rule; wording avoids requiring removal when another legal move is possible.
relation_note: Bearing off is explicitly the final removal process that completes backgammon's race.
relation_locator: Object of the Game; Bearing Off

label: Bar entry in backgammon
card: A lone backgammon checker hit by an opponent goes to the bar. Its owner must bring barred checkers back into the opponent's home board before moving other pieces. If the dice offer no open entry point, the player's turn is lost.
claim_review: USBGF Hitting and Entering supports hit, priority and failed entry; the chosen example concerns no available entry, not partial entry with several checkers.
relation_note: The rules make bar entry a compulsory recovery step after a checker is hit.
relation_locator: Hitting and Entering

label: Jacoby rule
card: The Jacoby rule is an optional backgammon scoring convention: a gammon or backgammon counts only as a single game unless a double has been offered. It removes the extra payoff for avoiding the cube merely to pursue a multiple-value win.
claim_review: USBGF Optional Rules explicitly labels Jacoby optional and states its incentive; do not apply it automatically to all match formats.
relation_note: The source explains Jacoby's purpose through whether players use the doubling cube during the game.
relation_locator: Optional Rules: The Jacoby Rule

label: Forced passing in Othello
card: Passing in Othello is compulsory when you cannot legally outflank an opposing disc, but forbidden when a legal move is available. Your opponent may therefore move twice in succession. If neither player can move, the game ends even when some squares remain empty.
claim_review: World Othello rules 2 and 8 support mandatory pass, prohibition of voluntary pass and early ending; no claim that every pass immediately ends play.
relation_note: The official game rules define passing entirely through legal outflanking moves.
relation_locator: Rules 2 and 8

label: Perpetual check in shogi
card: Repeated checking is not a safe route to a draw in shogi. Under the Japan Shogi Association's cited explanation, if continuous checks produce the same position four times, the player giving those checks loses. Ordinary repetition without continuous checking is treated differently.
claim_review: The official Japanese FAQ supports the fourth-occurrence loss and distinguishes ordinary repetition; the broad Shogi card instead explains piece reuse.
relation_note: The Japan Shogi Association identifies this as shogi's special treatment of repetition by continuous check.
relation_locator: FAQ: 連続王手の千日手というのは反則なのですか

label: Shogi impasse
card: Shogi's professional impasse procedure addresses positions with both kings advanced, no realistic mate and no further captures. Material is counted: rooks and bishops are worth five points, other nonking pieces one. If both players reach twenty-four points, the cited procedure requires a draw and replay.
claim_review: Japanese FAQ supports advanced kings, no mating prospect, no further captures, material values and twenty-four-point threshold; explicitly limited to its professional procedure, not every amateur or declaration rule.
relation_note: The official FAQ describes material-count adjudication as a shogi procedure and distinguishes professional from amateur variants.
relation_locator: FAQ: 持将棋の規定はどうなっていますか

label: Duplicate bridge
card: Duplicate bridge compares results from players holding the same deal of cards. A weak hand is therefore judged against what others achieved with that weak hand, rather than against opponents lucky enough to receive stronger cards. The format reduces the influence of the deal's initial luck.
claim_review: ACBL Duplicate Bridge supports identical deals and comparison against the field; reduces rather than eliminates chance, without claiming every duplicate scoring system is identical.
relation_note: ACBL presents duplicate as a bridge format in which the same deals are played at multiple tables.
relation_locator: Duplicate Bridge

label: Vulnerability in bridge
card: Vulnerability changes bridge's rewards and risks: successful contracts can earn higher bonuses, while failed contracts can incur greater penalties. In duplicate bridge, the board determines which partnership is vulnerable. This differs from rubber bridge, where winning a game changes a partnership's vulnerability.
claim_review: ACBL vulnerability definition supports premiums, undertrick penalties and the two different assignment methods; does not conflate vulnerable status with the strength of a hand.
relation_note: ACBL specifically explains how duplicate boards assign vulnerability independently of rubber-bridge game wins.
relation_locator: Scoring: Vulnerability

label: Dummy in bridge
card: After contract bridge's opening lead, the declarer's partner lays their hand face up as dummy. The declarer chooses which cards to play from both partnership hands. This creates a distinctive information pattern: defenders can see one opposing hand, but not the declarer's concealed cards.
claim_review: ACBL Play supports timing, exposed dummy and declarer's control; the information consequence is directly entailed, without claiming defenders see each other's hands.
relation_note: The play instructions define dummy as a specific role within the declaring partnership.
relation_locator: Play: declaring side

label: Offside in association football
card: Being in an offside position is not itself an offence. Under the cited football law, punishment depends on becoming involved in active play after a teammate plays the ball. Receiving it directly from a goal kick, throw-in or corner kick creates no offside offence.
claim_review: IFAB Law 11 separates position and active involvement and lists three direct-receipt exceptions; card deliberately avoids exhaustive positional geometry and goalkeeper-contact timing nuances.
relation_note: IFAB identifies offside as Law 11 within association football's Laws of the Game.

label: Curveball aerodynamics
card: A spinning baseball can experience a sideways aerodynamic force that bends its path. NASA's simplified curveball model links the curvature to spin, speed and air density. It treats the path as a circular arc when drag and the resulting changes in the force are neglected.
claim_review: NASA Aerodynamic Force gives the spinning-ball force and explicitly states the approximation; retain model qualification rather than declaring every real pitch a circular arc.
relation_note: NASA explicitly explains the curveball through aerodynamic force acting on a spinning baseball.
relation_locator: Aerodynamic Force and trajectory equation

label: Altitude effects on baseball pitches
card: A curveball's behavior depends partly on the air around it. In NASA's simplified model, lower air density weakens the aerodynamic deflection of a spinning pitch, all else equal. High-altitude conditions can therefore make a curveball travel along a straighter path.
claim_review: NASA's equation discussion directly links lower density with larger curvature radius; all-else-equal and simplified-model language avoid unsupported prediction of every pitch or game statistic.
relation_note: The source derives the altitude effect as a particular prediction of its curveball trajectory model.
relation_locator: Predictions from the curvature equation

label: Knuckleball aerodynamics
card: A baseball's seams make its surface aerodynamically uneven. As their orientation changes during flight, the effective location and direction of aerodynamic forces can vary. NASA connects these unsteady forces with the knuckleball's erratic motion, rather than explaining it solely through a steady spin-generated curve.
claim_review: NASA Forces on a Baseball, Lift, supports seam-dependent pressure changes and erratic motion; contrast with its separate simplified curveball model is labeled editorial in the relationship.
relation_note: Contrasting seam-sensitive, time-varying forces with a regular spinning-ball model separates two different explanations of curved baseball flight.
relation_locator: Forces on a Baseball, Lift; Curveball Trajectory, Aerodynamic Force

label: Topspin
card: Topspin helps a tennis ball dip into the court after clearing the net, allowing a faster shot to remain in play. Producing it depends on the racket's upward motion relative to the incoming ball, its tilt, and the ball's existing motion and spin.
claim_review: Cross's Ball Spin discussion supports dipping trajectory and multiple determinants; this is a tennis example of the registered generic topspin identity, not a novel application ID.
relation_note: Cross explicitly explains topspin production and its effect on shot trajectories in tennis.
relation_locator: 6 Ball Spin

label: Tennis racket sweet spot
card: A tennis racket's sweet spot is associated with reduced vibration reaching the hand. It does not necessarily coincide with the point of fastest ball rebound or zero total force on the hand. Rotation, translation and vibration contribute separately to what the player feels.
claim_review: Cross's Sweet spot section explicitly rejects both common identifications and lists three handle motions; do not equate the vibration node with an invariant center of percussion.
relation_target: Center of percussion in a tennis racket
relation_note: The source directly compares a vibration-node sweet spot with the separate center-of-percussion concept.
relation_locator: 1 Sweet spot; 3 Centre of percussion

label: Center of percussion in a tennis racket
card: An impact makes a tennis racket both recoil and rotate. At a particular supporting point, those motions can cancel. The corresponding impact location is its center of percussion. Adding the hand's mass shifts this relationship, so a freely suspended racket does not reproduce every playing condition.
claim_review: Cross's Centre of percussion section defines conjugate supporting and impact points and the hand-mass shift; this is not a universal fixed spot on every racket.
relation_note: Cross distinguishes cancellation of recoil and rotation from the separate vibration-node explanation of the sweet spot.
relation_locator: 1 Sweet spot; 3 Centre of percussion

label: Tennis racket dead spot
card: A ball dropped onto a suitably supported racket can stop almost dead after striking a particular location. Cross explains this through matching effective masses: the ball transfers its energy to the racket instead of rebounding strongly. The same location behaves differently when the racket is moving.
claim_review: Cross's Dead spot experiment supplies the support condition, effective-mass explanation and moving-racket contrast; avoid presenting this as an invariant no-rebound point in all strokes.
relation_note: Low rebound at a dead spot and reduced handle vibration at a sweet spot answer different questions about an impact.
relation_locator: 1 Sweet spot; 4 Dead spot

label: Drafting in cycling
card: A cyclist riding in another rider's wake can encounter less aerodynamic resistance and use less energy to maintain speed. The leading rider can also gain a smaller benefit. Road-racing groups exploit this shared airflow, although position and spacing affect how much shelter each rider receives.
claim_review: Exploratorium explains follower and leader advantages and spacing dependence; avoid exporting its numerical savings to all speeds, terrains or formations.
relation_note: The museum's Aerodynamics and Drafting explanation explicitly applies wake airflow to road cycling.
relation_locator: Drafting

label: Sweeping in curling
card: Curling sweepers influence a moving stone by working on the ice ahead of it. Pressure, brush angle and technique can affect how far it travels and how its path bends. World Curling's account emphasizes experimentation and acknowledges disagreement about the effectiveness of some techniques.
claim_review: World Curling's 2024 report supports distance, directional influence and uncertainty over knifing; it is a historical explanatory account, not a claim that all described techniques remain competition-legal in 2026.
relation_note: The governing body's report describes sweeping as a technique within curling that changes the stone's travel through surface work.
relation_locator: Sweeping techniques; Single sweeper

label: Rhythmic augmentation
card: Rhythmic augmentation stretches a musical idea in time while preserving its relative durations. A motive in quarter notes might return in half notes, with every value doubled. This differs from simply adding notes at the end: the existing pattern itself occupies more time.
claim_review: Puget Sound 11.2.3 defines usual proportional doubling; the contrast with extension is supported by 11.2.6. Preserve the registered rhythmic-augmentation control.
relation_note: The text explicitly presents diminution as the opposite temporal transformation to augmentation.
relation_locator: 11.2.3 Augmentation and Diminution

label: Musical diminution
card: Musical diminution shortens the rhythmic values of a motive or phrase, commonly by halving every duration. The pitch sequence can remain recognizable while the idea unfolds faster. Some uses of the term are less exact, referring more generally to a passage rewritten with shorter note values.
claim_review: Section 11.2.3 supports both exact halving and the broader usage; commonly prevents treating halving as an exceptionless definition.
relation_note: The textbook defines diminution in direct contrast with augmentation's usual doubling of durations.
relation_locator: 11.2.3 Augmentation and Diminution

label: Melodic retrograde
card: A melodic retrograde presents notes in the reverse order. It differs from melodic inversion, which reverses the direction of intervals rather than the sequence itself. Reading a tune backward and turning its upward leaps into downward leaps are therefore two distinct ways to transform musical material.
claim_review: Sections 11.2.7 and 11.2.1 support order reversal versus interval-direction reversal; no claim that retrograde necessarily reverses every performance parameter.
relation_note: Comparing the two definitions separates reversal of event order from reversal of melodic direction.
relation_locator: 11.2.1 Inversion; 11.2.7 Retrograde

label: Melodic inversion
card: Melodic inversion turns an idea's interval directions upside down. A rising movement becomes a falling one. Real inversion preserves the precise sizes and qualities of intervals, while tonal inversion adjusts them to fit the scale or key, allowing the transformed melody to remain within its tonal setting.
claim_review: Section 11.2.1 explicitly distinguishes real and tonal inversion; the tonal-setting consequence restates its scale/key qualification rather than claiming every interval is unchanged.
relation_note: Inversion changes interval direction; retrograde changes note order, so their labels should not be treated as aliases.
relation_locator: 11.2.1 Inversion; 11.2.7 Retrograde

label: Appoggiatura
card: An appoggiatura is a non-chord tone approached by a leap and left by a step. It is usually accented, placing the dissonance on a strong moment before resolution. The resolving step can go upward or downward; the expressive effect does not require one fixed direction.
claim_review: Puget Sound 10.4 supports leap approach, step departure, usual accent and either resolution direction; maintain its analytical sense rather than every historical ornamental use of the term.
relation_note: Both can create accented non-chord tension, but an appoggiatura arrives by leap whereas a suspension is prepared by the same note.
relation_locator: 10.4 Appoggiatura; 10.9 Suspension

label: Pedal point
card: A pedal point holds one note while surrounding harmonies change. It begins as a chord tone but can become a non-chord tone against later chords. Often heard in the bass, it can also appear higher up, creating continuity while its harmonic meaning shifts.
claim_review: Puget Sound 10.8 supports changing harmonic status, frequent bass placement and upper-voice pedals; the card does not restrict the device to a literal organ pedal.
relation_note: Both can sustain a note across a harmonic change, but the pedal persists across harmonies while a suspension has a prepared stepwise resolution.
relation_locator: 10.8 Pedal Point; 10.9 Suspension

label: Suspension in tonal music
card: A suspension carries a prepared note into a moment where it becomes an accented non-chord tone, then resolves downward by step. Its three stages are preparation, suspension and resolution. Labels such as 4–3 describe the changing interval above the bass rather than the note's absolute pitch.
claim_review: Section 10.9 supports preparation, accent, downward step and numbered intervals; bass suspensions have a special reference voice, so the card uses the ordinary 4–3 example.
relation_note: A suspension is approached by the same note, whereas an appoggiatura is approached by leap; their accented tension does not make them identical.
relation_locator: 10.9 Suspension; 10.4 Appoggiatura

label: Cadential six-four chord
card: A cadential six-four contains the notes of a tonic triad with its fifth in the bass, yet commonly functions as part of a dominant arrival. Before the following dominant chord, its pitch content and its harmonic role therefore point in different analytical directions.
claim_review: Puget Sound 16.3 explicitly identifies I6/4 preceding V and its dominant function; commonly avoids asserting that every second-inversion tonic is a cadential six-four.
relation_note: This sonority illustrates how harmonic function can differ from a chord's apparent tonic pitch content.
relation_locator: 16.3 The Cadential Six-Four Chord

label: Additive minimalism
card: Additive minimalism develops music by expanding repeated material in small steps. In Glass's examples, repetitions may be added or chords given extra subdivisions. The listener can follow a process of gradual growth rather than waiting for an entirely new theme to replace the existing pattern.
claim_review: Section 35.1 supplies Two Pages, Music in Fifths and lengthened chords in Einstein on the Beach; this describes the demonstrated processes rather than all minimalist composition.
relation_note: The textbook uses Glass's Two Pages as an explicit example of additive process combined with subtraction within repetitions.
relation_locator: 35.1 Additive Minimalism, opening example

label: Musical phase shifting
card: Phase shifting changes the alignment of repeated musical patterns. One part can retain its timing while another gradually runs ahead, or a performer can jump directly to the next rotation. Reich's Piano Phase and Clapping Music demonstrate these different ways of reorganizing the same recurring material.
claim_review: Section 35.2 explicitly contrasts gradual speeding in Piano Phase with discrete rotations in Clapping Music; no claim that both works require continuous tempo drift.
relation_note: The textbook explicitly identifies Piano Phase as a live-performance application of Reich's phase-shifting process.
relation_locator: 35.2 Phase Shifting

label: Tonal answer in fugue
card: A fugue's answer is a subject entry associated with the dominant key. In a tonal answer, some intervals are changed to accommodate the movement between tonic and dominant. A real answer instead preserves the intervals, making tonal function and literal transposition different possible priorities.
claim_review: Fugue Analysis defines answer, tonal modification and real preservation; associated with dominant leaves room for an answer beginning in tonic before moving there.
relation_note: The answer is explicitly defined as a structural element of a fugue's subject-entry process.
relation_locator: 30.8 answer definition

label: Countersubject
card: A countersubject is recurring counterpoint that accompanies a fugue's subject. Its identity matters: the composer brings back recognizable accompanying material when the subject returns, rather than inventing completely different counterpoint each time. The same countersubject can appear in different voices as the texture changes.
claim_review: Fugue Analysis defines consistent accompaniment and identifies one countersubject in alto and soprano; no requirement that every fugue have one is imposed.
relation_note: The source defines countersubject specifically within its fugue analysis and contrasts it with nonrecurring accompaniment.
relation_locator: 30.8 countersubject definition and BWV 847 example

label: Pitch (music)
card: Pitch is a sound's perceived highness or lowness. On a piano, moving right produces higher notes. For periodic musical tones, doubling the vibration frequency raises pitch by an octave, showing why musical intervals depend on frequency ratios rather than equal additions of hertz.
claim_review: Puget Sound 1.1 supports keyboard direction; UNSW's pitch discussion supplies periodic-tone frequency and octave ratio. Keep this auditory meaning separate from material pitch.
relation_note: Perceived pitch is the dimension being compared; concert pitch is a reference used to coordinate performers' tuning, not a synonym for that dimension.
relation_locator: Puget Sound 1.1; UNSW FAQ, Pitch, frequency, harmonics and missing fundamental

label: Inharmonicity of musical strings
card: Real instrument strings are not perfectly flexible. Their bending stiffness shifts higher vibration modes farther from exact whole-number multiples of the fundamental. This inharmonicity is especially relevant to plucked or struck strings; periodic bowing can instead draw the vibration into a harmonic pattern.
claim_review: UNSW harmonics discussion supports stiffness and stronger high-mode shifts, with the bowed versus plucked/struck qualification; not every real string is claimed equally inharmonic.
relation_note: The article explicitly contrasts inharmonic string resonances with harmonic motion enforced by bow-driven mode locking.
relation_locator: Real-string stiffness; stick-slip and mode-locking paragraphs

label: Mode locking in bowed strings
card: A bow alternately sticks to and slips against a string, sustaining a nearly periodic motion. That nonlinear drive can pull the string's slightly mismatched resonances into harmonic frequency ratios. The resulting steady note can therefore be more harmonically regular than the freely vibrating string's natural modes.
claim_review: UNSW explicitly attributes harmonic locking to periodic stick-slip drive; can and steady note preserve its operating-condition qualification.
relation_note: The source explains mode locking as the reason bowed motion can be harmonic despite slightly inharmonic natural resonances.
relation_locator: Stick-slip and mode-locking paragraphs

label: String harmonic
card: Lightly touching a string at a suitable point suppresses vibrations incompatible with a node there, bringing out a higher mode. Natural harmonics use an open string. Artificial harmonics combine stopping the string with a second light touch, giving the player access to different starting pitches.
claim_review: UNSW Strings explains touch-created nodes and open versus stopped strings; the second touch is not pressed firmly against the fingerboard.
relation_note: The cited violin touch-fourth example makes string-harmonic production a concrete performance technique for a bowed string instrument.
relation_locator: Strings, Harmonics and modes; Harmonics in music

label: Sympathetic resonance
card: An untouched guitar string can vibrate when another string is plucked. Harmonic components pass through the bridge and excite a compatible resonance in the second string. The apparent response at a distance therefore involves transferred mechanical energy and matched frequencies, not a second deliberate pluck.
claim_review: UNSW's guitar exercise explicitly links the low E string, bridge and B or high E strings; compatible resonance avoids asserting every string responds equally to every note.
relation_note: Shared harmonic frequencies help explain which unplayed strings respond, connecting resonance transfer with the harmonic modes used by performers.
relation_locator: Strings, guitar exercise before Harmonic tuning; Harmonics in music

label: Clapping Music
card: In Steve Reich's Clapping Music, rhythmic alignment changes through discrete rotations of a repeated pattern. One performer maintains the original pattern while the other moves to the next alignment on a measure's downbeat. Unlike Piano Phase, the transition does not require gradually speeding up.
claim_review: Puget Sound 35.2 directly names the work and discrete-rotation contrast; do not describe its shifting as continuous tape-style drift.
relation_note: The textbook identifies Clapping Music as a live-performance phase-shifting example using discrete rotations.
relation_locator: 35.2 rotation comparison

label: Piano Phase
card: Steve Reich's Piano Phase makes a repeating twelve-note pattern change through alignment rather than replacement. A second pianist gradually increases speed relative to the other part, causing the patterns to slip out of phase. The process lets different combinations emerge from recurring material.
claim_review: Section 35.2 supports the twelve-note pattern and second pianist's gradual speed change; emergent combinations follow from changing alignment, without an unsupported claim about exact complete formal design.
relation_note: The source explicitly presents the work as Reich's application of phase shifting to live pianists.
relation_locator: 35.2 Piano Phase example and rotation comparison

label: Two Pages
card: In Philip Glass's Two Pages, growth comes from adding repetitions, but successive copies lose their final notes. A motive can therefore be extended while the newly added units become shorter. The piece demonstrates how repetition and subtraction can work together within an additive process.
claim_review: The textbook's opening analysis states that each added repetition subtracts the previous repetition's final note; it labels the displayed notation a transcription, not the published score.
relation_note: The textbook names Two Pages as its opening example of Glass's additive process.
relation_locator: 35.1 opening example

label: Einstein on the Beach
card: The Train scene in Philip Glass's Einstein on the Beach provides a concrete example of additive process. A five-chord progression gradually lengthens as each chord receives more subdivisions. Musical change comes from stretching the allotted duration of recurring harmonies rather than continuously introducing new chords.
claim_review: Puget Sound 35.1 describes the named scene, five chords and added subdivisions; the claim is limited to that example, not the entire opera.
relation_note: The source explicitly recommends the Train scene as an example of additive growth in chord duration.
relation_locator: 35.1 Act 1, Scene 1, Train

label: Bach's Fugue in C minor, BWV 847
card: Bach's C-minor fugue from the first Well-Tempered Clavier offers a compact lesson in contrapuntal development. Its opening exposition introduces the subject in every voice. Episodes then work with smaller fragments of subjects and countersubjects, allowing recognizable material to generate passages without a complete subject statement.
claim_review: The detailed analysis identifies first exposition, all-voice entries and fragmented material in episodes; no unsupported numerical count of voices or episodes is added.
relation_note: The source explicitly analyzes BWV 847 as a fugue with expositions and episodes.
relation_locator: 30.8 first exposition and first episode

label: Bach's Invention in C major, BWV 772
card: Bach's C-major Invention shows how a short idea can sustain development. The opening notes return with their melodic direction inverted, and fragments also appear in rhythmic augmentation. These transformations preserve recognizable material while changing its contour or the amount of time it occupies.
claim_review: Section 11.2 identifies the first seven notes inverted later and an augmented fragment; the wording does not claim every occurrence transforms the whole theme.
relation_note: The textbook explicitly labels the invention's returning opening notes as melodic inversion.
relation_locator: 11.2.1 Bach example; 11.2.3 augmentation example

label: Adagio for Strings
card: Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings supplies a textbook example of a 4–3 suspension. A prepared note remains while the harmony changes, creating a dissonant fourth above the bass before stepping down to a third. The delayed resolution makes harmony unfold through the movement of individual voices.
claim_review: The suspension chapter explicitly labels its Barber example 4–3; general preparation and stepwise resolution come from the same section. No unsupported emotional or biographical claim is added.
relation_note: The named score example is explicitly introduced as a 4–3 suspension.
relation_locator: 10.9 definition and Figure 10.9.3

label: Neapolitan chord
card: The Neapolitan chord is a major chord built on the lowered second scale degree. In classical tonal analysis it commonly appears in first inversion and serves a predominant function. Its distinctive chromatic color therefore has a directional role, helping prepare the approach to dominant harmony.
claim_review: Section 20.1 names flat II, most-common first inversion and predominant function; major quality follows the uppercase chord notation, not a claim that every flat-II sonority has this function.
relation_note: The Neapolitan's predominant role contrasts with the cadential six-four's dominant role, despite both often occurring near a cadence.
relation_locator: 20.1 Neapolitan definition; 16.3 Cadential Six-Four Chord

label: Augmented sixth chord
card: An augmented sixth chord places two voices a semitone on either side of the dominant scale degree. The raised fourth moves upward while the lowered sixth moves downward toward that goal. This converging chromatic motion explains the chord family's predominant role in the cited tonal framework.
claim_review: Puget Sound 21.1 gives raised fourth, lowered sixth and simultaneous approach to five; the paragraph describes scale-degree tendencies, not an unrestricted claim about every voicing or historical style.
relation_note: Both are chromatic predominant devices, but their pitch construction differs: converging semitones versus a lowered-supertonic major triad.
relation_locator: 21.1 Augmented Sixth Chords; 20.1 The Neapolitan Chord

label: Species counterpoint
card: Species counterpoint organizes practice in combining melodies through controlled rhythmic relationships. A learner might write one, two, three or four notes against a longer note in another voice. The constraints isolate different problems of coordination before more freely varied contrapuntal textures are attempted.
claim_review: Puget Sound 30.1 supports the rhythmic species and educational framing; the final sentence is a modest explanation of the controlled-practice structure, not a claimed universal learning outcome.
relation_note: The textbook explicitly presents species counterpoint as a method for learning contrapuntal composition.
relation_locator: 30.1 Species Counterpoint

label: Counterpoint
card: Counterpoint combines two or more melodic lines sounding at the same time. A listener can follow their separate motion while also hearing the resulting texture. This differs from organizing the music principally as one foreground melody with accompaniment, a contrast the textbook calls contrapuntal versus homophonic.
claim_review: Puget Sound 30.1 supplies simultaneous melodic lines and the texture contrast; independent motion is not taken to mean harmonic unrelatedness.
relation_note: The same section identifies species as a structured approach to composing counterpoint.
relation_locator: 30.1 Species Counterpoint

label: Missing fundamental
card: A small loudspeaker may reproduce a bass note's upper harmonics while barely producing its lowest frequency. Listeners can nevertheless hear the corresponding low pitch. For periodic tones, the spacing between surviving harmonics supplies information about the absent fundamental, so perceived pitch need not match the lowest audible component.
claim_review: UNSW FAQ explains periodic-tone pitch from harmonic spacing and the bass-speaker example; it does not claim that arbitrary inharmonic sounds imply a unique missing fundamental.
relation_note: The source uses the missing fundamental to distinguish perceived pitch from the presence of a lowest-frequency component.
relation_locator: FAQ, Pitch, frequency, harmonics and missing fundamental

label: Stretch tuning
card: Piano octaves are often tuned slightly wider than a strict two-to-one frequency ratio. Stiff strings have upper partials sharper than ideal harmonics. Matching the upper note to a lower string's second partial can reduce audible beating, making a mathematically exact octave a poor practical match.
claim_review: UNSW FAQ gives stretched second partials and beat-eliminating tuning; often and can avoid prescribing one exact stretch for every piano or register.
relation_note: The FAQ explicitly explains stretched tuning as a response to stiffness-induced inharmonicity in struck piano strings.
relation_locator: FAQ, What is stretch tuning?

label: Tartini tone
card: Two notes can give rise to an additional difference tone at the difference between their frequencies. Called a Tartini tone in music, it can result from nonlinear interactions in an instrument or the hearing system. The extra perceived pitch need not be one of the two notes originally played.
claim_review: UNSW discusses difference-frequency combination tones and multiple possible nonlinear sources; can avoids attributing every case to one anatomical or instrumental mechanism.
relation_note: A difference tone involves nonlinear frequency combination, whereas sympathetic resonance transfers energy into a compatible existing resonance; the comparison distinguishes two additional-sound phenomena.
relation_locator: FAQ, Heterodyne and combination tones; Strings, guitar sympathetic-vibration exercise

label: Just intonation
card: Just intonation favors intervals described by simple frequency ratios. Yet pure fifths and pure thirds do not fit every chain of notes identically: repeated three-to-two fifths can conflict with a pure third. Fixed-pitch instruments must therefore confront compromises that adjustable voices or strings can handle differently.
claim_review: UNSW temperament discussion supplies the chain-of-fifths mismatch and fixed versus adjustable instrument distinction; no claim that one tuning is universally best.
relation_note: The FAQ directly contrasts just intonation with meantone's compromise between thirds and fifths.
relation_locator: FAQ, What is all the fuss about temperament?

label: Meantone temperament
card: Meantone temperament narrows fifths to improve the tuning of major thirds. The discrepancy is distributed across a chain of fifths rather than left entirely in the resulting third. This can suit particular keys well, while movement into other keys exposes the compromise's limits.
claim_review: UNSW's worked example describes thirds improved by narrowing four fifths and worsening problems in other keys; no relation is made to personality temperament Q80157.
relation_note: The cited tuning comparison presents meantone as a different way to reconcile pure-interval demands on fixed-pitch instruments.
relation_locator: FAQ, What is all the fuss about temperament?

label: Wind-instrument end correction
card: An open pipe behaves acoustically as though it extends slightly beyond its physical opening. The air's motion spreads outward before the pressure reflection develops, increasing the effective vibrating length. A resonance therefore occurs slightly lower than a simple model using only the measured tube length predicts.
claim_review: UNSW End effects explains delayed reflection and effective length; slightly and simple model preserve the approximation rather than asserting one universal correction distance.
relation_note: End corrections qualify ideal pipe predictions, including the simplified boundary-condition model used to explain clarinet register spacing.
relation_locator: Open vs Closed Pipes, Standing wave diagrams and End effects

label: Clarinet overblowing at the twelfth
card: A simple clarinet model is a cylindrical pipe closed at one end, which supports an odd-harmonic sequence. Its next resonance is therefore near three times the fundamental, a musical twelfth higher. Real clarinets depart from the ideal cylinder, but the model explains their characteristic register jump.
claim_review: UNSW explicitly compares closed and open pipes and cautions that bore, bell, mouthpiece and end corrections complicate real instruments; no exact all-register harmonic claim.
relation_note: The article directly applies the closed-pipe approximation to clarinet register behavior.
relation_locator: Standing wave diagrams; Frequency analysis; real-instrument qualifications

label: Prepared piano
card: A prepared piano changes its sound through objects placed beneath or between its strings. John Cage used such physical alterations to expand the instrument's available timbres. The keys remain a familiar interface, while the altered vibrating system produces sounds unlike those of an unprepared grand piano.
claim_review: John Cage Trust explains objects placed among a grand piano's strings and the resulting transformed instrument; no invented preparation materials or exact acoustic mechanism is specified.
relation_note: The Trust explicitly connects its prepared-piano samples with materials used for Cage's Sonatas and Interludes.
relation_locator: Prepared piano app description

label: Glass armonica
card: Benjamin Franklin's glass armonica uses glass bowls of different sizes mounted on a spinning axle. A player's touch sustains their vibration through friction, much as a damp finger can make a glass rim sing. The instrument turns that small physical effect into a playable arrangement of pitches.
claim_review: UNSW wineglass explanation names Franklin, rotating bowls and finger-driven stick-slip; no claim about exact construction dimensions or historical priority beyond the source.
relation_note: The source compares rubbing glass with a violin bow's sticking and slipping, providing a factual basis for comparing friction-driven sound production.
relation_locator: FAQ, Why does rubbing a finger around a wine-glass rim make a note?; Harmonics, bow-string stick-slip

card: John Cage's 4′33″ directs attention toward sounds already present around a performance. The John Cage Trust's official app makes this idea concrete by recording ambient sound in three movements. The example shifts attention from supplying a new melody to noticing the listening environment itself.
claim_review: The Trust's description supports ambient listening and its three-movement app realization; wording does not infer every original score instruction from the app or claim literal absence of sound.
relation_note: The Trust identifies this as Cage's composition; its ambient-sound focus offers a boundary-testing example of musical listening.
relation_locator: 4′33″ official app description

label: Sonatas and Interludes
card: Cage's Sonatas and Interludes, composed in 1946–48, uses a prepared piano whose strings are altered by inserted materials. The John Cage Trust later supervised samples made with the work's actual preparation materials, linking the composition's identity to a particular physically modified sound source.
claim_review: The Trust gives dates, work title and supervised sampling using actual preparation materials; no unsupported list of objects or formal analysis of the cycle is added.
relation_note: The official description explicitly identifies the work's piano preparations as the basis for its supervised sampled sounds.
relation_locator: Prepared piano app description

label: Gradus ad Parnassum
card: Johann Joseph Fux's Gradus ad Parnassum, published in 1725, teaches contrapuntal composition through species counterpoint. Its historical importance includes organizing melodic combination into constrained rhythmic exercises. Comparing one note against a longer note with several notes against it reveals the organizing idea behind that approach.
claim_review: Puget Sound names Fux, date and species pedagogy; the explanatory comparison comes from the section's species definitions, not a claim about every exercise in the original book.
relation_note: The textbook explicitly states that Fux's work teaches composition through species counterpoint.
relation_locator: 30.1 opening paragraph

label: Memory
card: Memory involves several activities rather than a single recording process. Encoding organizes incoming information, storage retains it, and retrieval brings it back for use. Remembering a fact later therefore depends on more than exposure: the information must have been encoded and remain accessible when needed.
claim_review: OpenStax 8.1 defines encoding, storage and retrieval; the final consequence follows that sequence without claiming a literal computer-like architecture is complete.
relation_note: The chapter explicitly includes procedural skill memory among the forms of long-term memory.
relation_locator: 8.1 opening; Long-Term Memory

label: Working memory model
card: Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory model treats temporary mental activity as more than a single storage box. A central executive coordinates specialized systems for verbal and visual-spatial material. The later addition of an episodic buffer illustrates that this is a developing explanatory model, not an immutable anatomical diagram.
claim_review: OpenStax 8.1 names the executive, subsystems and Baddeley 2000 buffer addition; explicitly a model, without unsupported localization or claims that the buffer belonged to the 1974 formulation.
relation_note: The chapter introduces this as an alternative explanatory model of memory's short-term organization.
relation_locator: 8.1 Storage

label: Sensory memory
card: Sensory memory briefly holds information from sights, sounds and other sensory events. In the Atkinson–Shiffrin model, this fleeting store precedes short-term memory. The distinction explains why a sensory trace can exist momentarily without becoming something retained for later conscious recall.
claim_review: OpenStax 8.1 Sensory Memory supports brief traces and model placement; preserve the baseline's original description separately rather than silently replacing its wording.
relation_note: The textbook explicitly describes sensory memory as a stage within a model of memory storage.
relation_locator: 8.1 Storage; Sensory Memory

label: Self-reference effect
card: The self-reference effect is a relative memory advantage for information connected to oneself. Material considered in personally relevant terms can be remembered better than less self-relevant material. It is studied as an influence on encoding, linking what information means to a person with later remembering.
claim_review: OpenStax Encoding defines the relative advantage and places it after semantic-processing experiments; can avoids an exceptionless guarantee or an instructional prescription.
relation_note: The textbook explicitly introduces self-reference as an effect on encoding and subsequent memory.
relation_locator: 8.1 Encoding, self-reference paragraph

label: Procedural memory
card: Procedural memory is expressed in skilled actions, such as balancing on a bicycle or driving. Practice can improve performance even when a person cannot fully describe the knowledge guiding it. This distinguishes remembering how to do something from consciously reporting facts or past events.
claim_review: OpenStax Long-Term Memory defines implicit procedural skill and contrasts reportable explicit memories; not every component of driving is claimed unconscious.
relation_note: Molaison's preserved improvement despite impaired new declarative memory provides a concrete comparison between performance-based and consciously reportable remembering.
relation_locator: 8.1 implicit procedural memory; 8.3 Anterograde Amnesia

label: Proactive interference
card: Proactive interference occurs when older learning gets in the way of remembering newer information. After changing phone numbers, you might keep giving the old number automatically. The direction matters: an established memory is obstructing access to its more recently learned replacement.
claim_review: OpenStax 8.3 defines old-to-new interference and gives the phone-number example; this concerns retrieval competition, not proof that the new memory was erased.
relation_note: The source explicitly distinguishes the two forms by whether older or newer information interferes.
relation_locator: 8.3 Interference

label: Retroactive interference
card: Retroactive interference occurs when newer learning makes older information harder to recall. After learning a replacement address, you might struggle to recover the previous one. The direction reverses proactive interference: what was learned later now obstructs access to what was learned earlier.
claim_review: OpenStax 8.3 defines new-to-old interference and depicts new and old email addresses; harder to recall does not assert permanent erasure.
relation_note: The chapter presents retroactive and proactive interference as opposite directions of interference between old and new learning.
relation_locator: 8.3 Interference

label: Source-monitoring error
card: A source-monitoring error confuses where remembered information came from. Someone might remember seeing a film accurately but assign that experience to the wrong companion. The mistake concerns the memory's origin or context, showing why recognizing a familiar detail does not guarantee correct attribution.
claim_review: OpenStax misattribution example supports wrong companion/context. Only registered Q7565103 is used; no second meaning is asserted for Q6875176 and no silent baseline merger occurs.
relation_note: Confusing a remembered source differs from incorporating misleading later information, although both can distort reports about an event.
relation_locator: 8.3 errors of distortion and The Misinformation Effect

label: Misinformation effect
card: Later information can alter how an earlier event is remembered. In Loftus and Palmer's car-crash studies, wording in questions affected speed estimates and later reports of broken glass. The finding shows how post-event suggestions can shape reports, rather than proving that every eyewitness memory is inaccurate.
claim_review: OpenStax describes both question wording and later glass reports; studies plural avoids treating the different experimental stages as one undifferentiated sample.
relation_note: These are different routes to memory distortion: external post-event suggestion versus confusion over a detail's source.
relation_locator: 8.3 The Misinformation Effect; errors of distortion

label: Henry Molaison
card: Henry Molaison, known in research as H. M., had severe difficulty forming new declarative memories after brain surgery. Yet he could improve at repeatedly practiced tasks without remembering previous practice. His case separates conscious memory for an episode from learning expressed through better performance.
claim_review: PubMed abstract of Augustinack et al. directly identifies Henry Molaison as H. M.; OpenStax 8.2 supports surgery and declarative impairment, and 8.3 supports improved performance without recalled practice. Do not claim all old memories remained intact.
relation_note: The textbook explicitly uses H. M. to contrast impaired new episodic/semantic memory with preserved procedural learning.
relation_locator: 8.2 Hippocampus; 8.3 Anterograde Amnesia

label: Absolute sensory threshold
card: An absolute sensory threshold is usually defined as the stimulus intensity detected on half of repeated presentations under specified conditions. It is therefore a probabilistic measurement, not a magical boundary below which detection never happens. The testing conditions matter when comparing how sensitive different observers appear.
claim_review: OpenStax 5.1 supplies the fifty-percent criterion and controlled conditions; probabilistic interpretation follows that definition without importing unsupported exact sensitivity estimates.
relation_note: A detection percentage alone does not separate available sensory information from a decision criterion; signal detection theory analyzes that distinction.
relation_locator: 5.1 absolute threshold; Heeger, Information and Criterion

label: Just-noticeable difference
card: A just-noticeable difference measures the change needed to distinguish two stimulus intensities. The same added light can be conspicuous in a dark room yet barely noticeable in bright surroundings. This differs from asking whether any light can be detected at all, the question behind an absolute threshold.
claim_review: OpenStax 5.1 contrasts difference and absolute thresholds using dark versus bright settings; avoid treating Weber's approximate scaling as universal across every intensity range.
relation_note: The textbook explicitly distinguishes detecting a stimulus from detecting a difference between stimuli.
relation_locator: 5.1 Sensation, absolute and difference thresholds

label: Sensory adaptation
card: With prolonged stimulation, a continuing sensory input can become less noticeable even while it remains present. OpenStax describes this as sensory adaptation. The change highlights a gap between continuing stimulation and conscious experience, helping explain why an initially prominent feature of the surroundings can fade from awareness.
claim_review: OpenStax's perception section explicitly describes reduced notice during continued stimulation; this phenomenological card does not assert a particular receptor mechanism or equate every attention lapse with adaptation.
relation_note: Reduced notice of sustained input differs from missing a visible unexpected event while concentrating on another task.
relation_locator: 5.1 sensory adaptation and selective-attention passages

label: Inattentional blindness
card: Inattentional blindness is missing a visible event while attention is occupied elsewhere. In the basketball-pass counting demonstration described by OpenStax, many viewers failed to notice an unexpected gorilla-costumed figure. The result concerns divided task demands, not an inability of the eyes to receive the image.
claim_review: OpenStax 5.1 gives the counting task and unexpected figure; many avoids transferring one condition's numerical rate to every observer or task.
relation_note: Both concern limits of attention, but this card concerns an unexpected visible event during another task, rather than two targets arriving close together in time.
relation_locator: 5.1 selective-attention study; pinned attentional-blink identity distinction

label: Signal detection theory
card: Signal detection theory separates available evidence from the criterion used to decide that a signal is present. Lowering the criterion can increase both hits and false alarms; raising it can reduce both. Better sensitivity and a greater willingness to answer yes are therefore different kinds of change.
claim_review: Heeger's actual Information and Criterion and criterion-shift passages support the distinction and tradeoff. This is a theory of uncertain decisions, not a synonym for detection ability.
relation_note: A fifty-percent detection threshold summarizes responses, while signal detection theory distinguishes evidence quality from the criterion behind those responses.
relation_locator: Heeger, Information and Criterion; OpenStax 5.1 absolute threshold

label: Figure–ground (perception)
card: Figure–ground organization separates a focal object from its background. In the familiar vase-and-faces image, the same boundary can outline a white vase or two dark faces. Changing which region counts as the figure changes what the image seems to depict.
claim_review: Section 5.6, figure-ground paragraph and Figure 5.25, support segmentation and the reversible vase/faces example; the card avoids claiming that segmentation must always precede recognition.
relation_note: Compare selecting an object against its background with perceptually completing an incomplete object; these are distinct operations illustrated in the same Gestalt discussion.
relation_locator: Section 5.6, figure-ground relationship and closure, Figures 5.25 and 5.29

label: Perceptual closure
card: Perceptual closure is the tendency to see a complete object from incomplete visual parts. Broken arcs can look like a circle rather than unrelated segments. The perceived whole therefore contains an organization that is not supplied by a continuous drawn outline.
claim_review: Section 5.6, closure definition and Figure 5.29, explicitly contrast whole circles and rectangles with fragmented segments; this is a perceptual tendency, not a guarantee for any broken image.
relation_note: Closure fills an incomplete whole, whereas good continuation favors smooth trajectories; comparing their illustrations prevents treating all visual grouping as one mechanism.
relation_locator: Section 5.6, continuity and closure paragraph, Figures 5.28–5.29

label: Good continuation
card: Good continuation is a visual grouping tendency: lines that form a smooth path are more likely to be perceived as belonging together than jagged, broken alternatives. It helps explain why an arrangement of separate marks can appear organized into continuous trajectories.
claim_review: Section 5.6 calls continuity a tendency toward smooth flowing lines; the card keeps probabilistic wording and does not claim a compulsory rule of vision.
relation_note: The continuity and closure examples invite comparison between following a smooth path and completing an object from missing pieces, without identifying the two principles.
relation_locator: Section 5.6, law of continuity and principle of closure

label: Mental set
card: A mental set is persistence with a problem-solving approach that worked before but is ineffective now. Familiarity can keep a solver repeating the same strategy instead of reconsidering the problem. Functional fixedness is a particular case involving an object's expected use.
claim_review: Section 7.3 defines persistence with an earlier successful approach and explicitly calls functional fixedness a type of mental set; no claim that all learned routines are harmful.
relation_note: The source explicitly identifies functional fixedness as a type of mental set, narrowing a habitual strategy to assumptions about object use.
relation_locator: Section 7.3, Pitfalls to Problem Solving, mental set and functional fixedness paragraphs

label: Functional fixedness
card: Functional fixedness restricts thinking about an object to its usual purpose. In Duncker's candle problem, seeing a box only as a container can obscure its use as a candle support. Overcoming that restriction requires reconsidering what the available materials can do.
claim_review: Section 7.3, Duncker problem and Figure 7.10, support the box's alternative use; the prose avoids repeating the source's apparent typo about using fixedness to overcome the problem.
relation_note: The source expressly describes functional fixedness as a kind of mental set: a familiar use constrains the attempted solution.
relation_locator: Section 7.3, Pitfalls to Problem Solving, Duncker example

label: Anchoring effect
card: Anchoring occurs when one piece of information receives disproportionate weight in judgment. A house hunter may fixate on an initial spending figure and overlook what that amount actually buys. The focal value narrows consideration even when other relevant information is available.
claim_review: Section 7.3's housing-budget example supports overfocus on a focal amount; this card does not claim a measured universal numerical adjustment effect from that example alone.
relation_note: Compare overreliance on a focal information point with reliance on a readily accessible example; both can narrow consideration, but their selection mechanisms differ.
relation_locator: Section 7.3, anchoring paragraph and availability heuristic paragraph

label: Confirmation bias
card: Confirmation bias makes evidence supporting an existing belief easier to notice than evidence challenging it. Someone convinced a teacher is unfriendly may remember curt exchanges while overlooking pleasant ones. The resulting impression can feel well supported because counterexamples received less attention.
claim_review: Section 7.3's professor example supports selective attention to confirming episodes; retain authored control local:authored:000049 and its prior version, with Q431498 left as a historical equivalence proposal rather than a second meaning.
relation_note: Confirmation bias favors evidence fitting a prior belief; the availability heuristic favors accessible examples. This comparison separates two reasons an evidence sample may be selective.
relation_locator: Section 7.3, confirmation bias and availability heuristic paragraphs

label: Hindsight bias
card: Hindsight bias is the tendency to see a known outcome as having been predictable beforehand. Learning what happened changes the perspective from which an earlier decision is judged. Confidence after the event can therefore be mistaken for foresight that was never actually demonstrated.
claim_review: Section 7.3 defines hindsight as retrospective predictability; the temporal contrast is explanatory paraphrase, not a claim that every correct retrospective explanation is biased.
relation_note: Hindsight concerns a known outcome's apparent predictability; confirmation concerns selecting support for an existing belief. Their juxtaposition separates retrospective confidence from selective evidence use.
relation_locator: Section 7.3, confirmation and hindsight definitions and Table 7.3

label: Availability heuristic
card: The availability heuristic uses readily accessible examples or recent experiences to guide judgment. That shortcut can be misleading when the easiest case to recall is poorly suited to the decision. Accessibility supplies an answer quickly, but does not establish that the example is representative.
claim_review: Section 7.3 explicitly says the available example may not best inform a decision; representativeness here means suitability of evidence, not the separate representativeness heuristic.
relation_note: A readily recalled case and a focal numerical amount can each dominate judgment for different reasons; the comparison does not merge the two biases.
relation_locator: Section 7.3, anchoring and availability definitions

label: Intrinsic motivation
card: Intrinsic motivation comes from satisfaction in the activity itself, such as baking because it is enjoyable. External rewards can also motivate the same person. Distinguishing these sources helps explain why turning a favorite activity into paid work can sometimes change its appeal.
claim_review: Section 10.1's intrinsic/extrinsic distinction and Odessa baking example support mixed motives and a possible change after payment; sometimes preserves the section's later qualifications.
relation_note: The section moves from intrinsic motivation to evidence that external rewards can change it, while distinguishing tangible rewards, praise and expectations.
relation_locator: Section 10.1, intrinsic/extrinsic opening and Odessa/reward discussion

label: Motivation crowding theory
card: External rewards can change intrinsic motivation rather than simply adding to it. Expected tangible rewards may weaken interest in an activity, while praise or an unexpected reward can have different effects. The finding depends on the reward and context, so payment does not invariably destroy enjoyment.
claim_review: Section 10.1 distinguishes expected tangible rewards, praise and surprise; the card retains Q6917879 and does not create a second overjustification identity or universal causal law.
relation_note: The reward discussion directly concerns increases or decreases in intrinsic motivation, making this an interaction with that motive rather than a separate definition of enjoyment.
relation_locator: Section 10.1, qualified external-reward effects

label: Yerkes–Dodson relationship
card: The Yerkes–Dodson relationship links arousal and performance while emphasizing task difficulty. A demanding task may be disrupted at an arousal level that suits a simple one. The useful lesson is not that moderate arousal always wins, but that an apparent optimum depends on the task.
claim_review: Section 10.1 explicitly qualifies the middle-is-best simplification through difficulty; the card states a relationship and qualified example rather than a universal biological law or prescriptive stress target.
relation_note: Compare performance's dependence on arousal and task difficulty with motivation's dependence on perceived capability; these are different explanations discussed in the motivation chapter.
relation_locator: Section 10.1, Arousal theory and Self-efficacy and Social Motives

label: Self-efficacy
card: Self-efficacy is a person's belief that they can carry out a particular task. In Bandura's account, this belief helps shape the challenges people attempt and their persistence after setbacks. Believing an outcome is valuable differs from believing one has the capability to achieve it.
claim_review: Section 10.1 defines task-specific capability beliefs and attributes their motivational role to Bandura; the card does not equate confidence with actual skill or guarantee success.
relation_note: Capability beliefs answer whether one can perform a task, whereas intrinsic motivation concerns satisfaction in doing it; the chapter supports both premises without identifying them.
relation_locator: Section 10.1, intrinsic motivation opening and Self-efficacy and Social Motives

label: Cognitive dissonance
card: Cognitive dissonance is discomfort associated with inconsistent beliefs, attitudes or behavior. Someone who smokes while believing smoking is harmful may reduce the conflict by quitting or by discounting the evidence. Resolving the discomfort can therefore involve changing behavior or changing its interpretation.
claim_review: Section 12.3's definition, smoking example and Figure 12.11 support both routes; the card avoids making the source's restrictive self-image formulation a universal necessary condition.
