relation_note: Discounting conflicting evidence can be compared with selectively attending to confirming evidence, but discomfort reduction and confirmation bias remain distinct explanatory subjects.
relation_locator: Section 12.3, smoking example; Section 7.3, confirmation bias

label: Elaboration likelihood model
card: The elaboration likelihood model distinguishes persuasion through evaluating a message's arguments from persuasion through peripheral cues. A buyer might compare safety evidence or respond to a celebrity endorsement. The model connects these routes with the audience's motivation and effort in processing the message.
claim_review: Section 12.3, Figure 12.15 and central/peripheral route paragraphs, support argument evaluation, endorsement cues and processing effort; the card identifies a model rather than an exhaustive settled binary for all persuasion.
relation_note: The model concerns how a persuasive message is processed; foot-in-the-door concerns the sequence of requests. Their comparison distinguishes explanatory route from influence procedure.
relation_locator: Section 12.3, Two Routes to Persuasion and Foot-in-the-door Technique

label: Foot-in-the-door technique
card: The foot-in-the-door technique begins with a small request before asking for something larger. In Freedman and Fraser's study, people who first accepted a small sign or petition were more likely to accept a large yard sign. This was an experimental tendency, not guaranteed compliance.
claim_review: Section 12.3 describes the 1966 sign/petition comparison; the final sentence preserves probabilistic scope and avoids presenting a guaranteed method of controlling another person.
relation_note: Compare a request-sequencing procedure with a model of message processing. Both concern persuasion, but the cited section does not make one an instance of the other.
relation_locator: Section 12.3, Foot-in-the-door Technique and Two Routes to Persuasion

label: Asch's conformity experiments
card: In Asch's line-judgment experiments, participants heard a group give an obviously wrong answer before responding aloud. Many agreed with the group at least once. Dissenting allies and private responding changed conformity, showing that agreement depended partly on the social arrangement of the task.
claim_review: Section 12.4 supports confederates' wrong answers, public responses and effects of dissent/privacy; many avoids generalizing one percentage to all studies or people.
relation_note: The textbook explicitly interprets conformity in the unambiguous Asch task as fitting in and avoiding ridicule, an instance of normative influence.
relation_locator: Section 12.4, Asch procedure and Why conform? normative influence paragraphs

label: Normative social influence
card: Normative social influence draws people toward a group's position because acceptance matters. Someone may publicly give an answer they privately doubt to avoid ridicule or fit in. Agreement in this case need not mean believing the group has better information about the question.
claim_review: Section 12.4 distinguishes fitting in from information-based conformity and notes public agreement without private acceptance in Asch's setting; the card allows rather than requires private disagreement.
relation_note: The text explicitly contrasts acceptance-seeking with trusting the group's information, identifying two different motivations for conformity.
relation_locator: Section 12.4, normative versus informational influence

label: Informational social influence
card: Informational social influence occurs when people treat others' responses as evidence about an uncertain situation. If smoke in a theater might be a special effect, nearby people's reactions can guide interpretation. Conformity here reflects reliance on presumed knowledge, rather than only a wish to belong.
claim_review: Section 12.4's ambiguous smoke example and competent-group definition support uncertainty-driven reliance; the hypothetical example is not presented as a measured emergency experiment.
relation_note: The textbook directly distinguishes believing the group is informed from seeking its acceptance, while allowing both as motivations for conformity.
relation_locator: Section 12.4, Why conform? and theater-smoke example

label: Milgram's obedience experiments
card: Milgram's participants believed they were administering increasingly strong shocks when an experimenter instructed them to continue; the learner actually received none. In the original setting, many continued to the highest level. Changing the setting or bringing the learner closer reduced obedience, limiting any simple universal conclusion.
claim_review: Section 12.4 describes the deceptive shock setup and lower continuation rates in office/proximity variants; no claim that all participants obeyed or that this settles explanations of historical atrocities.
relation_note: Milgram tests responses to an experimenter's commands, whereas Asch tests responses to a group's judgments. The comparison distinguishes authority-directed obedience from peer conformity.
relation_locator: Section 12.4, Asch procedure and Stanley Milgram's Experiment

label: Psychology
card: Psychology studies mind and behavior through empirical methods. Mental processes are not directly visible, so researchers draw inferences from behavior, biological indicators and people's reports. A claim about thought becomes scientifically testable by connecting it to observations that could support or challenge an explanation.
claim_review: Section 1.1 explicitly links indirect mental inference to observable behavior, biological indicators and self-report; the card does not imply that introspection alone proves a mental mechanism.
relation_note: Inferring an unobservable psychological process from a measure creates the construct-validity question: does that measure capture the intended concept? The two inspected sections supply these premises.
relation_locator: Section 1.1, empirical methods; Section 2.3, Reliability and Validity

label: Inter-rater reliability
card: Inter-rater reliability concerns agreement between observers evaluating the same event. If two researchers classify a behavior differently, the coding procedure may be inconsistent. Agreement helps establish reproducibility across observers, but by itself does not show that their shared measure captures the intended psychological construct.
claim_review: Section 2.3 defines observer agreement and distinguishes reliability from validity; the coding example applies that definition without claiming agreement proves accuracy.
relation_note: The source lists inter-rater and test–retest reliability as distinct consistency checks: across observers versus across administrations.
relation_locator: Section 2.3, Reliability and Validity, types of reliability

label: Test–retest reliability
card: Test–retest reliability asks whether a measure produces consistent results across repeated administrations. It evaluates stability over occasions, whereas inter-rater reliability evaluates agreement among observers. A repeatable score can still measure the wrong thing, so consistency alone does not establish the validity of its interpretation.
claim_review: Section 2.3 distinguishes repeated-administration consistency from observer agreement and states that reliability does not entail validity; the card does not demand unchanged scores when the actual trait changes.
relation_note: Both forms are explicitly listed in the same reliability passage, with different sources of variation being checked.
relation_locator: Section 2.3, Reliability and Validity, inter-rater and test-retest definitions

label: Construct validity
card: Construct validity asks whether a measure actually captures the concept it is intended to represent. A procedure can produce consistent scores yet miss its intended target. The challenge is therefore more than repeatability: it is connecting an observable measurement to the psychological idea being studied.
claim_review: Section 2.3 defines construct validity and separates validity from reliability; the card does not assert that surface plausibility or one correlation settles the question.
relation_note: The source explicitly contrasts measuring the intended construct with merely obtaining consistent results; observer agreement is one specified form of that consistency.
relation_locator: Section 2.3, Reliability and Validity

label: Ecological validity
card: In this research-methods sense, ecological validity concerns how well findings apply to ordinary settings. Unobtrusive observation of people in their usual surroundings can improve realism, but sacrifices experimental control. A realistic setting helps the applicability question without automatically answering every question about cause and effect.
claim_review: Section 2.2's naturalistic-observation discussion supports realism, generalization and control tradeoffs; retain this cited sense rather than treating all uses of ecological validity as interchangeable.
relation_note: Real-world applicability and accurate measurement of an intended construct are different validity questions; the comparison is a learning bridge, not a claim that one guarantees the other.
relation_locator: Section 2.2, Naturalistic Observation; Section 2.3, Reliability and Validity

label: Experimenter expectancy bias
card: A researcher's expectations can influence how ambiguous observations are scored. Someone who knows which participants received an intervention may interpret borderline responses in its favor. Concealing group assignments from the scorer helps reduce this route of bias, without guaranteeing that every other source of error disappears.
claim_review: Section 2.3's test-scoring example motivates observer blinding; helps reduce avoids the textbook's stronger implication that blinding alone removes all alternative explanations.
relation_note: The source introduces researcher blinding to address experimenter expectations and then defines double blinding as concealing assignment from participants as well.
relation_locator: Section 2.3, Causality, experimenter bias and double-blind paragraphs

label: Double-blind study
card: In a double-blind study, participants and the relevant researchers do not know which group each participant belongs to. Concealing assignments helps limit both participant expectations and experimenter expectations. It is a protection against those influences, not a substitute for sound sampling, measurement or comparison groups.
claim_review: Section 2.3 defines concealed assignment for researchers and participants; the final limitation follows the chapter's separate design requirements and avoids claiming that blinding alone demonstrates causation.
relation_note: Double blinding is directly introduced as controlling both experimenter and participant expectations, so its relation to expectancy bias is stated rather than inferred.
relation_locator: Section 2.3, Causality, double-blind definition and purpose

label: Research debriefing
card: Research debriefing explains a study after participation, especially when its purpose was concealed. Participants receive an honest account of the research question, the use of their data and why deception was used. The explanation helps restore information that the study deliberately withheld during the task.
claim_review: Section 2.4 explicitly requires a full explanation after deceptive studies, including purpose, data use, reasons and further information; the card does not promise that explanation erases any harm.
relation_note: The ethics passage makes debriefing a requirement following deception and specifies the information participants should receive.
relation_locator: Section 2.4, Research Involving Human Participants, deception and debriefing

label: Deception in psychological research
card: Psychological studies sometimes conceal their precise purpose because knowing it could change participants' responses. That creates an ethical tension between informative behavior and informed participation. The cited ethics account limits deceptive procedures and requires a later explanation of the purpose, data use and reasons for concealment.
claim_review: Section 2.4 explains response distortion and debriefing, with ethical limits; the card attributes this account and does not treat scientific convenience as sufficient permission for harmful deception.
relation_note: The source directly connects permissible use of deception with a subsequent full debriefing rather than treating concealment as an unrestricted research tool.
relation_locator: Section 2.4, deception example and mandatory debriefing paragraph

label: Social desirability bias
card: Social desirability bias can make self-reports reflect how people want to appear rather than what they actually do or believe. A respondent might underreport drinking to seem more acceptable. This is one possible source of inaccurate survey answers, alongside memory errors and other influences.
claim_review: Section 2.2's surveys paragraph explicitly separates lying, misremembering and answers intended to look good; the card does not diagnose every inaccurate response as deliberate dishonesty.
relation_note: Social desirability concerns the participant's presentation of an answer, whereas experimenter expectancy concerns the researcher's interpretation; contrasting them separates two locations where measurement can be distorted.
relation_locator: Section 2.2, Surveys; Section 2.3, Causality, experimenter bias

label: Doctrine of double effect
card: The doctrine of double effect distinguishes harm intended as a means from harm foreseen as a side effect of pursuing a good end. Its defenders also require proportionality and attention to avoiding harm. Merely saying a bad result was unintended does not make it permissible.
claim_review: SEP sections 1 and 3 support the intention/foresight distinction, proportionality and harm minimization; attribution to defenders avoids presenting a contested doctrine as settled morality.
relation_note: The entry explicitly warns that intended versus foreseen harm is a different distinction from doing versus allowing harm; neither distinction should be substituted for the other.
relation_locator: Double Effect, section 3 Misinterpretations

label: Problem of closeness in double effect
card: The problem of closeness challenges the line between intended means and foreseen side effects. A harmful result may be so closely connected with an agent's chosen means that calling it unintended seems artificial. The difficulty is classifying the action without already assuming the moral verdict.
claim_review: SEP section 4.2 identifies closely connected harms, and 4.3 raises evaluation-driven descriptions; the card presents a criticism rather than declaring that every intention distinction collapses.
relation_note: The entry names the problem of closeness as a criticism of double effect's distinction between intended means and merely foreseen harms.
relation_locator: Double Effect, sections 4.2 The Problem of Closeness and 4.3 The Side Effect Effect

label: Doing versus allowing harm
card: Doing harm and allowing harm distinguish bringing about a harmful outcome from failing to prevent it. Philosophers dispute their moral significance. Rachels's paired cases compare deliberate drowning with deliberately withholding rescue, testing whether the distinction alone can explain a difference in blame.
claim_review: SEP sections 1–2 present Rachels's cases and objections to both their comparability and generalization; the card treats the cases as a test, not proof that killing and letting die are always equivalent.
relation_note: The entry uses driver and bystander trolley variants to examine whether doing/allowing explains moral judgments, and records challenges to that explanation.
relation_locator: Doing vs. Allowing Harm, section 3

label: Trolley problem
card: The trolley problem asks whether redirecting a lethal threat from five people toward one is permissible. Changing the decision-maker from driver to bystander challenges explanations based simply on doing versus allowing harm. The variants probe moral distinctions rather than supply an agreed algorithm for sacrifice.
claim_review: SEP section 3 recounts Foot's driver and Thomson's bystander variants and continuing disagreement; no endorsement of a universal permissibility verdict or practical sacrifice rule is made.
relation_note: The bystander variant is explicitly discussed as a challenge to Foot's doing/allowing explanation of the driver's choice.
relation_locator: Doing vs. Allowing Harm, section 3, Foot and Thomson discussion

label: Moral luck
card: Moral luck names a tension in judging people: responsibility seems to require control, yet praise and blame often depend on factors outside their control. Two equally reckless actions can have different outcomes. The puzzle asks whether, and how, those differences should affect moral assessment.
claim_review: SEP's Control Principle and resultant-luck examples support the tension; the card asks rather than settles the normative question and does not create an additional resultant-luck identity.
relation_note: The entry identifies circumstantial luck as one form of moral luck, involving which situations a person happens to face rather than only how an action ends.
relation_locator: Moral Luck, The Problem and Types of luck

label: Problem of temporary intrinsics
card: The problem of temporary intrinsics asks how one persisting object can have incompatible intrinsic properties at different times. A metal plate may change from round to square. Explaining that change requires an account of what it means to possess a property at a time.
claim_review: SEP Identity Over Time sections 2.3–2.4 use the plate's shape change and discuss competing solutions; the card does not infer that ordinary change is logically impossible.
relation_note: The section explicitly frames the temporary-intrinsics problem through Leibniz's Law: identity and differing properties require explaining the temporal qualification.
relation_locator: Identity Over Time, section 2.3 Leibniz's Law and the Possibility of Change

label: Circumstantial moral luck
card: Circumstantial moral luck concerns the unchosen situations that test a person's character. Someone placed in a brutal political environment may face choices another person never encounters. The philosophical problem is whether differing moral assessments are justified when the opportunity for wrongdoing itself depended on luck.
claim_review: SEP's circumstantial-luck paragraph compares collaborators with imagined counterparts elsewhere; the card generalizes that structure without excusing atrocities or asserting that circumstances compel every action.
relation_note: Nagel's taxonomy in the entry expressly treats luck in one's circumstances as a kind of moral luck affecting assessment.
relation_locator: Moral Luck, Types of luck, Circumstantial luck

label: Constitutive moral luck
card: Constitutive moral luck concerns traits and dispositions shaped partly by factors people did not choose, including inheritance and upbringing. If those traits influence action, judging someone's character also raises a question about control. The issue is responsibility for who one has become, not merely what happens afterward.
claim_review: SEP's constitutive-luck paragraphs identify genes, caregivers and peers, and connect dispositions with action; partly avoids a deterministic claim that character or conduct is wholly unchosen.
relation_note: The source explicitly classifies luck in character and dispositions as constitutive moral luck, extending the control problem to agents as well as actions.
relation_locator: Moral Luck, Types of luck, Constitutive luck

label: Supererogation
card: Supererogation is morally good action beyond what duty requires. A costly rescue may be admired even when failing to undertake it would not violate an obligation. Whether such optional goodness forms a genuine category is disputed, because some ethical theories make every morally best action compulsory.
claim_review: SEP opening and Definition discuss good-but-not-required acts, heroic examples and theories denying the category; costly rescue is an illustration, not a requirement that every supererogatory act be costly.
relation_note: The entry explicitly distinguishes optional action beyond duty from imperfect duties, which remain binding while allowing discretion over fulfillment, and notes attempts to equate them.
relation_locator: Supererogation, section 2 Definition, imperfect-duty discussion

label: Imperfect duty
card: In the Kantian distinction discussed here, an imperfect duty remains obligatory while leaving latitude in how it is fulfilled. Flexibility about particular actions does not make the underlying duty optional. This separates discretion within an obligation from supererogation, which concerns morally good action beyond obligation.
claim_review: SEP section 2 explicitly says imperfect duties are no less compelling and differ in application; the opening bounds this formulation to the Kantian discussion rather than every use of the term.
relation_note: The article contrasts imperfect duty's binding force and discretionary application with supererogatory optionality; it also acknowledges philosophers who dispute that separation.
relation_locator: Supererogation, section 2, imperfect duties and Kant

label: Suberogation
card: Suberogation is a proposed category of morally bad but permissible conduct, conceived as a counterpart to good actions beyond duty. Ingratitude is sometimes offered as an example, but both the examples and the category are disputed. Badness and prohibited wrongdoing need not be treated as identical.
claim_review: SEP section 2 describes the proposed mirror category, contested ingratitude example and difficulty identifying clear cases; proposed and sometimes preserve its disputed status.
relation_note: The source introduces suberogation by asking whether supererogation has a mirror image, then examines why the suggested symmetry is controversial.
relation_locator: Supererogation, section 2, offence and suberogation

label: Justified true belief analysis
card: The justified true belief analysis proposes that knowledge requires a belief to be true and adequately justified, with those conditions together sufficient. Truth excludes error; justification excludes unsupported lucky guesses. Gettier cases challenge the proposal by combining justification and truth with another kind of epistemic luck.
claim_review: SEP sections 1 and 3 describe the tripartite proposal and its challenge; proposes and challenge prevent the analysis from being presented as the settled definition of knowledge.
relation_note: The entry explicitly presents Gettier counterexamples as a challenge to the sufficiency of justification, truth and belief together.
relation_locator: The Analysis of Knowledge, sections 1 and 3

label: Gettier problem
card: The Gettier problem asks why some justified true beliefs still seem not to be knowledge. A person can reason from a justified but false premise to a conclusion that happens to be true for an unrelated reason. The success is accidental despite the apparent justification.
claim_review: SEP section 3's Smith/Jones disjunction case supports justified false premise, valid inference and accidental truth; some and seem preserve the philosophical status of the counterexample judgment.
relation_note: Gettier cases are directly formulated as counterexamples to the traditional tripartite analysis, separating justified truth from nonaccidental knowledge.
relation_locator: The Analysis of Knowledge, section 3 Counterexamples to the Tripartite Analysis

label: No-false-lemmas condition
card: The no-false-lemmas condition proposes repairing justified true belief by excluding beliefs inferred from false premises. It blocks some Gettier examples, but deceptive perceptual environments pose a further challenge. A belief can apparently be accidentally true without having been inferred from any false proposition.
claim_review: SEP section 4 states the proposed fourth condition and noninferential counterexamples; the card does not claim the repair is accepted or sufficient.
relation_note: The entry expressly develops no false lemmas as an attempted additional condition for solving the Gettier problem, then presents objections.
relation_locator: The Analysis of Knowledge, section 4 No False Lemmas

label: Fake-barn case
card: In the fake-barn case, Henry happens to see a real barn in a landscape full of convincing facades. His belief is true and apparently justified, yet could easily have been mistaken. The example challenges whether accurate perception alone guarantees knowledge in a systematically deceptive environment.
claim_review: SEP section 4's Barn County passage supplies Henry, the real barn and facades; apparently and challenges preserve the evaluative character of the knowledge verdict.
relation_note: The source presents Barn County as a challenge to the no-false-lemmas repair because Henry's belief need not involve inference from a false premise.
relation_locator: The Analysis of Knowledge, section 4, Barn County

label: Epistemic sensitivity
card: A sensitive belief tracks a counterfactual question: if the claim were false, would the person stop believing it? A mirage-based belief may fail because the same appearance would persuade without water. Sensitivity has been proposed as a condition on knowledge, but its adequacy is disputed.
claim_review: SEP section 5.1 states the counterfactual and desert-water example, then discusses limitations; the card does not equate sensitivity with safety or endorse it as sufficient for knowledge.
relation_note: Section 5.2 explicitly contrasts sensitivity with safety and explains why counterfactual contraposition does not make them equivalent.
relation_locator: The Analysis of Knowledge, sections 5.1 and 5.2

label: Epistemic safety
card: A safe belief would not easily have been false: in nearby possible circumstances where the person holds it, it remains true. This proposed condition on knowledge differs from asking what the person would believe if the claim were false. What counts as nearby is itself contested.
claim_review: SEP section 5.2 gives the nearby-worlds formulation and discusses vagueness of nearness; the card avoids treating safety as a settled necessary or sufficient condition.
relation_note: The source explicitly distinguishes safety's nearby true beliefs from sensitivity's response to falsity, noting that the two modal conditions are not equivalent.
relation_locator: The Analysis of Knowledge, section 5.2 Safety

label: Epistemic closure
card: Epistemic closure asks whether competent deduction preserves knowledge. On a common formulation, someone who retains knowledge of a premise and comes to believe its consequence by competent deduction knows that consequence. This is not a claim that people automatically know every implication of everything they know.
claim_review: SEP section 1 rejects unqualified entailment closure and gives the competent-deduction principle with continued premise knowledge; the card presents a formulation within a disputed debate.
relation_note: Knowledge preservation under inference is a specific epistemological question; the closure entry and the broad account of cognitive success support this placement without implying universal acceptance of closure.
relation_locator: Epistemic Closure, section 1; Epistemology, opening account of cognitive success

label: Lottery paradox
card: If high probability licenses belief, each ticket in a large fair lottery may reasonably be treated as a loser. Combining all those beliefs yields that every ticket loses, although one must win. The lottery paradox challenges combining individually plausible beliefs without restriction.
claim_review: SEP section 3 presents Kyburg's acceptance rule and agglomeration conflict; the conditional opening avoids asserting that probability alone actually suffices for rational belief or knowledge.
relation_note: The article introduces the preface paradox as a companion challenge to agglomeration, while noting that it does not require the same probabilistic acceptance rule.
relation_locator: Epistemic Paradoxes, sections 3 and 4

label: Preface paradox
card: An author can reasonably believe each carefully researched claim in a book while admitting that the book probably contains an error. Combining all the individual beliefs conflicts with that admission. The preface paradox tests how rational confidence in particular claims fits with recognition of one's fallibility.
claim_review: SEP section 4 explains Makinson's author case and its conflict with agglomeration; the card preserves rational belief rather than recasting every assertion as knowledge or certainty.
relation_note: The source connects both paradoxes through agglomeration while distinguishing the preface's ordinary recognition of fallibility from a numerical probability-acceptance rule.
relation_locator: Epistemic Paradoxes, sections 3–4

label: Moore's paradox
card: Moore's paradox concerns the oddness of asserting a fact while denying that one believes it. The combination need not be logically contradictory: someone else could truthfully describe that situation. The puzzle is why the speaker's own present assertion appears to undermine the position it expresses.
claim_review: SEP section 5.3 distinguishes first-person declarative oddity from third-person, conditional and past-tense counterparts; the card avoids calling the proposition itself a formal contradiction.
relation_note: Both expose tensions involving belief, but Moore's case centers on an assertion's first-person stance, whereas the preface case concerns combining individually rational beliefs.
relation_locator: Epistemic Paradoxes, sections 4 and 5.3

label: Meno's paradox of inquiry
card: Meno's paradox asks how inquiry can work: if you already know the answer, inquiry seems unnecessary; if you do not, how could you recognize it? One response distinguishes partial knowledge from total ignorance. A searcher may know enough to recognize an answer without already possessing it.
claim_review: SEP section 6.1 states the dilemma and partial-knowledge response; one response avoids presenting it as the only interpretation of Plato or the final resolution of all inquiry puzzles.
relation_note: A puzzle about gaining and recognizing knowledge belongs within epistemology's study of cognitive success; the bridge uses the inquiry passage and the field's inspected overview.
relation_locator: Epistemic Paradoxes, section 6.1; Epistemology, opening overview

label: Epistemology
card: Epistemology investigates knowledge, justification, understanding and other kinds of cognitive success. It asks how evidence should constrain belief and what separates knowing from merely being right. Different approaches examine individual reasoning, sensory experience or the social interests that influence which evidence receives attention.
claim_review: SEP's opening survey explicitly discusses knowledge versus true opinion, sensory justification, formal evidence constraints and feminist attention to interests; the card avoids reducing the field to one proposed knowledge analysis.
relation_note: The tripartite analysis is one particular attempt to explain knowledge within a broader field that also studies justification, understanding and evidence; it is not the definition of epistemology itself.
relation_locator: Epistemology, historical overview; The Analysis of Knowledge, section 1

label: Numerical and qualitative identity
card: Numerical identity means being one and the same thing; qualitative identity means being alike in qualities. The distinction matters for change: a persisting object can remain the same object while its features alter. Similarity of appearance alone does not settle whether two descriptions pick out one thing.
claim_review: SEP Identity Over Time section 1 distinguishes one object from exact resemblance and connects persistence with qualitative change; the card does not assume the controversial converse identity-of-indiscernibles principle.
relation_note: The introduction moves directly from numerical/qualitative identity to Leibniz's Law, exposing the need to explain how qualitative change fits identity through time.
relation_locator: Identity Over Time, section 1 Introduction

label: Indiscernibility of identicals
card: The indiscernibility of identicals says that if two names pick out the very same thing, every property of that thing must belong to both referents. It runs from identity to shared properties. The converse claim, that sharing all properties guarantees identity, is a different principle.
claim_review: SEP section 1 explicitly distinguishes identity implying indiscernibility from the converse; the two-name formulation explains reference without suggesting that differing descriptions themselves prove distinct objects.
relation_note: The entry states Leibniz's Law after distinguishing numerical from qualitative identity, and separately names its more controversial converse.
relation_locator: Identity Over Time, section 1, Leibniz's two principles

label: Relative identity
card: Relative identity proposes that asking whether two things are the same requires specifying the kind of thing: the same what? On Geach's view, things might be the same under one classification but different under another. This contested proposal challenges treating identity as a single unqualified relation.
claim_review: SEP Identity Over Time section 1 attributes sortal-relative identity to Geach and contrasts it with absolute identity; proposes and contested prevent endorsing it as standard logic.
relation_note: Compare ordinary numerical identity with a proposal that identity must be qualified by a sortal. This is a competing analysis, not another name for qualitative similarity.
relation_locator: Identity Over Time, section 1, numerical identity and Geach's sortal proposal

label: Material constitution
card: A clay statue raises a puzzle: the clay seems able to survive squashing, while the statue does not. Does that show two coincident objects, or should their relationship be understood differently? Material constitution investigates this disputed relationship between an object and the matter that constitutes it.
claim_review: SEP opening and section 1 present the statue/lump persistence argument alongside identity and revisionary views; seems and the question explicitly avoid settling the dispute in favor of two objects.
relation_note: The statue-and-clay argument explicitly invokes Leibniz's Law: if their persistence properties differ, identity is threatened. The entry presents rival responses rather than endorsing that inference without qualification.
relation_locator: Material Constitution, section 1, The Puzzle of the Statue and the Clay

label: Presentism
card: Presentism holds that only temporally present objects exist. Merely past or future objects are excluded from its inventory of reality, though abstract entities may fall outside time. The claim concerns existence itself, not simply which events people can currently observe or remember.
claim_review: SEP Time section 6 defines presentism and explicitly distinguishes temporal presence from spatial presence and timeless abstract objects; no claim that the past never occurred.
relation_note: The source directly opposes presentism to eternalism, which includes objects at past and future times in what exists.
relation_locator: Time, section 6 Presentism, Eternalism, and the Growing Block Theory

label: Eternalism
card: Eternalism holds that past and future objects exist as well as present ones. Existing need not mean being located at the present time, just as occupying another place need not mean being nowhere. The view separates an object's temporal location from whether it belongs to reality.
claim_review: SEP Time section 6 separates ontological existence from present temporal location and includes past/future objects; the spatial comparison restates the distinction, not a claim that all eternalists endorse one spacetime theory.
relation_note: Section 6 explicitly defines eternalism as a way of opposing presentism's restriction of existence to present objects.
relation_locator: Time, section 6, temporal-location and ontological senses of existence

label: Growing block theory
card: Growing block theory holds that the past and present exist, while the future does not yet exist. Reality expands as new events join its present edge. It differs from presentism, which excludes the past, and eternalism, which includes future objects in what exists.
claim_review: SEP Time section 6 defines the increasing ontology and contrasts both alternatives; the card does not equate the growing block with four-dimensionalism or a settled physical theory.
relation_note: The section contrasts eternalism's past-and-future existence with the growing block's past-and-present existence, marking the future as their key difference.
relation_locator: Time, section 6, growing block paragraph

label: Sorites paradox
card: The sorites paradox turns tiny changes into a puzzle about vague categories. If one grain is not a heap, and adding one grain never makes the difference, repeated additions seem to imply that no heap is possible. Plausible small steps produce an unacceptable conclusion.
claim_review: SEP opening and section 2 supply the grain-addition chain; the card identifies the conflict without asserting that the tolerance premise is true or resolving vagueness by definition.
relation_note: The entry presents epistemicism as one response to the sorites paradox, locating a sharp but unknowable boundary rather than accepting every small-step premise.
relation_locator: Sorites Paradox, opening and section 3.2

label: Epistemicism about vagueness
card: Epistemicism treats vagueness as a limit of knowledge rather than an absence of precise boundaries. There is, on this view, an exact cutoff between a heap and a non-heap, although we cannot identify it. Statements remain true or false even when their status is inaccessible.
claim_review: SEP section 3.2 describes hidden sharp boundaries and preservation of bivalence; on this view makes the controversial account explicit rather than reporting it as a discovered linguistic fact.
relation_note: The article presents epistemicism among responses to sorites, preserving classical bivalence while denying that every adjacent pair must share the same status.
relation_locator: Sorites Paradox, section 3.2 The Epistemic Theory

label: Supervaluationism
card: Supervaluationism evaluates a vague statement across admissible ways of making its terms precise. A statement true under every such interpretation is supertrue; some borderline statements are neither supertrue nor superfalse. This permits truth-value gaps while preserving many classical logical laws, including excluded middle.
claim_review: SEP section 3.3.1 defines admissible precisifications, supertruth and gaps while discussing retained classical laws; the card does not equate semantic indeterminacy with epistemic ignorance.
relation_note: The entry explicitly contrasts supervaluationism's semantic indeterminacy with epistemicism's unknown but sharp boundaries; this comparison explains their different treatments of borderline cases.
relation_locator: Sorites Paradox, sections 3.2 and 3.3.1

label: Two truths in Indian Buddhist philosophy
card: Indian Buddhist discussions of two truths distinguish conventional understanding from an ultimate perspective. Ordinary language and practices operate conventionally, while ultimate analysis asks how things really are. Buddhist schools interpret both levels and their relationship differently, so the distinction does not express one uniform doctrine across traditions.
claim_review: SEP opening differentiates conventional and ultimate perspectives and explicitly warns that the schools can be radically opposed; the card avoids attributing one settled metaphysics or historical origin to all Buddhism.
relation_note: The distinction concerns perspectives on truth and knowledge, inviting comparison with epistemology's study of cognitive success without assimilating all Buddhist schools to a single Western theory.
relation_locator: The Theory of Two Truths in India, opening and schools overview; Epistemology, opening

label: Zhuangzi’s butterfly dream
card: Zhuangzi's butterfly dream reverses the security of waking identity: was Zhuangzi dreaming of a butterfly, or is a butterfly dreaming of Zhuangzi? In the cited interpretation, the story encourages modesty about one's present perspective. Feeling released from an earlier error need not establish a final standpoint.
claim_review: SEP's discussion around Zhuangzi 2:14 links the story to perspectival shifts and mild skepticism; in the cited interpretation avoids claiming one uncontested reading or that the story proves reality illusory.
relation_note: The dream provides a literary route into questions about certainty and cognitive perspective; this is an editorial learning bridge, not a claim that Zhuangzi adopted a modern epistemological doctrine.
relation_locator: Zhuangzi, epistemic reflection around 2:12–2:14; Epistemology, cognitive success overview

label: Political science
card: Political science examines collective choices and conflicts, especially those involving government. A useful analysis asks which rules apply, what circumstances participants face and what choices they make. The same formal rule can produce different outcomes when the surrounding conditions or participants' strategies change.
claim_review: OpenStax section 1.1 defines government-focused collective interactions and the rules/reality/choices framework; the final sentence expresses their interaction rather than a quantified causal finding.
relation_note: The chapter identifies a constitution as the most basic legal rules structuring government, one important instance of the rules its political-analysis framework examines.
relation_locator: Introduction to Political Science 1.1, Rules and constitutional principles

label: Constitution (politics)
card: A political constitution sets out basic principles governing public power, including institutional structure, governmental duties and people's rights. Those principles need not appear in a single document. Constitutional arrangements can combine written provisions with other sources, so a state's constitution is more than a document's title.
claim_review: OpenStax section 1.1 identifies constitutional structure, duties and rights and gives multi-source examples; no claim that every constitutional guarantee is effectively enforced.
relation_note: The passage explicitly distinguishes constitutional functions from having a single constitutional document, with the UK among its examples.
relation_locator: Introduction to Political Science 1.1, constitutional principles and multi-document examples

label: Parliamentary sovereignty
card: Parliamentary sovereignty is the UK's principle that Parliament is the supreme legal authority and can make or repeal laws. One Parliament cannot generally prevent a later Parliament from changing its legislation. Institutional reforms may constrain how power is exercised without, in this account, extinguishing that legal principle.
claim_review: UK Parliament's sovereignty page states supremacy, future repeal and reforms; generally and in this account preserve the official explanation's legal qualifications and avoid denying practical political constraints.
relation_note: The official page presents sovereignty as a central principle of the UK's partly written, uncodified constitution, directly connecting principle and constitutional form.
relation_locator: Parliamentary sovereignty, opening, UK constitution and Developments sections

label: Uncodified constitution
card: An uncodified constitution lacks one consolidated constitutional text, not necessarily written rules. The United Kingdom's constitutional arrangements include many statutes alongside other sources. Calling the constitution unwritten can therefore mislead: the important distinction is whether its basic rules are collected in a single authoritative document.
claim_review: UK Parliament's sovereignty page expressly describes the constitution as partly written and wholly uncodified; the card does not equate uncodified with informal, unenforceable or absent.
relation_note: The page identifies uncodified as the form of the UK's constitution, while explaining that many constitutional rules are nevertheless written in statutes.
relation_locator: Parliamentary sovereignty, Parliamentary sovereignty and the UK constitution

label: Parliament Act 1911
card: The Parliament Act 1911 followed conflict over the Lords' rejection of the 1909 budget. It replaced the Lords' veto over most Commons public bills with delay, while protecting bills extending Parliament's lifetime. A later Act in 1949 shortened that delaying power, showing how legislative authority shifted between chambers.
claim_review: UK Parliament's history and exceptions sections support the budget conflict, qualified veto reduction and later 1949 change; most Commons public bills avoids applying the procedure to every bill.
relation_note: The official explanation sets the Act within normal Commons–Lords agreement and specifies circumstances where one chamber's consent can be bypassed.
relation_locator: The Parliament Acts, opening, historical background and excluded bills

label: Salisbury convention
card: The Salisbury convention restrains the House of Lords from voting down government bills promised in an election manifesto. It helps an elected government advance its announced program even without a Lords majority. This convention concerns how a chamber exercises its powers, rather than a new statutory voting procedure.
claim_review: UK Parliament's Salisbury section states manifesto-bill restraint and lack of a Lords majority; describing it as a convention distinguishes the source's separate account of statutory Parliament Acts procedures.
relation_note: Compare a political convention limiting opposition to manifesto bills with a statutory route around Lords consent; both affect inter-chamber relations but operate through different mechanisms.
relation_locator: The Parliament Acts, statutory procedure and The Salisbury Convention

label: Money bills under the Parliament Acts
card: Under the UK Parliament Acts, a Speaker-certified money bill can reach Royal Assent without Lords consent after a month without unamended passage. It must already have passed the Commons and reached the Lords at least a month before session-end; the Commons can direct otherwise.
claim_review: The Parliamentary Counsel guidance, paragraphs 1.2, 1.5, 1.8 and 2.2, supplies certification and all timing/direction conditions; this supersedes the introductory page's misleading claim of automatic assent within a month and its absolute amendment claim.
relation_note: The guidance expressly identifies section 1 of the 1911 Act as the money-bill procedure and reproduces its legal conditions.
relation_locator: Money Bills, paragraphs 1.1–1.8 and 2.2, reproduced Parliament Act 1911 section 1

label: Bicameralism
card: Bicameralism organizes a legislature into two chambers. In the United Kingdom, the Commons and Lords normally both pass a bill before it becomes law, but the Parliament Acts create specified exceptions. The example shows that two chambers need not possess equal or unrestricted blocking powers.
claim_review: UK Parliament's opening describes two-house agreement and exceptions; the card confines the mechanics to the UK and does not universalize its unequal powers across all bicameral systems.
relation_note: The Parliament Acts page directly explains the two chambers' ordinary role through the statutory exceptions that modify it.
relation_locator: The Parliament Acts, opening and Bills subject/not subject to the Parliament Acts

label: Mixed-member proportional representation
card: Mixed-member proportional representation combines constituency representatives with party-list seats intended to make overall representation proportional. In New Zealand's version, voters choose a local candidate and a party separately. The party vote largely determines each party's total seats, while electorate winners take individual constituency seats.
claim_review: New Zealand Electoral Commission's MMP explanation supports separate votes and the overall party share; intended and largely accommodate allocation qualifications, and New Zealand's version prevents universalizing its exact rules.
relation_note: The official MMP explanation identifies the threshold as the New Zealand eligibility rule operating within this electoral system, not as a universal property of MMP.
relation_locator: What is MMP?, Two votes and Political parties try to win party votes and electorate votes

label: New Zealand MMP threshold
card: New Zealand's MMP system gives parties two routes to parliamentary eligibility: at least five percent of the party vote or an electorate victory. The alternative route means a party below the percentage threshold can still qualify through local success. These are New Zealand's rules, not universal MMP requirements.
claim_review: The Electoral Commission explicitly states the five-percent or electorate-seat alternatives; the card does not claim an exact seat entitlement or apply the threshold to other countries.
relation_note: The official page locates the threshold within New Zealand's MMP allocation and explains it alongside separate party and electorate votes.
relation_locator: What is MMP?, Political parties try to win party votes and electorate votes

label: Confidence and supply agreement
card: A confidence and supply agreement allows one party to support another on specified parliamentary matters without forming a coalition government together. New Zealand's electoral authority distinguishes these arrangements from parties joining government. The distinction shows that keeping a government functioning need not mean sharing its entire program.
claim_review: The Electoral Commission's Parties negotiate section differentiates coalition membership from support on certain issues/laws; the card does not claim all agreements have identical terms or require support on every bill.
relation_note: The New Zealand MMP explanation discusses confidence and supply as one arrangement parties may negotiate when no party can govern alone, not an inevitable consequence of MMP.
relation_locator: What is MMP?, Parties negotiate to form a government

label: Constructive vote of no confidence
card: Germany's constructive vote of no confidence requires the Bundestag to elect a successor Chancellor by a majority of its members while seeking the incumbent's dismissal. Opposition must therefore agree on a replacement, not merely on rejection. Article 67 also requires forty-eight hours between motion and election.
claim_review: Basic Law Article 67 supplies majority membership, successor election, dismissal request and waiting period; the institutional consequence follows those express conditions and is bounded to Germany.
relation_note: Compare Germany's constitutional replacement requirement with New Zealand's negotiated support arrangements. Both concern parliamentary support for government, but one is a removal procedure and the other an interparty agreement.
relation_locator: Basic Law Article 67; What is MMP?, Parties negotiate to form a government

label: German eternity clause
card: Germany's eternity clause makes certain constitutional amendments inadmissible, including changes affecting the federal division into Länder and principles protected by Articles 1 and 20. This differs from merely requiring a large majority: Article 79 sets substantive limits that the ordinary two-thirds amendment procedure cannot override.
claim_review: Basic Law Article 79(2)–(3) distinguishes two-thirds votes from inadmissible amendments; including avoids claiming that the examples exhaust the clause, and no universal claim about all constitutions is made.
relation_note: The clause exemplifies a constitutional limit on the power to amend basic governmental rules; the Basic Law provision and general constitution account support that editorial placement.
relation_locator: Basic Law Article 79; Introduction to Political Science 1.1, constitutional principles

label: Concurrent legislative powers in Germany
card: In Germany's concurrent legislative sphere, the Länder generally may legislate while the Federation has not exercised its power. Federal legislation can therefore change the space for state action. Article 72 also permits departures in specified fields, so concurrency does not mean either unrestricted coexistence or uniform federal exclusion.
claim_review: Basic Law Articles 70–72, reinspected through all of Article 72, support the general rule and paragraph 3 exceptions; generally and specified fields avoid falsely absolute federal displacement.
relation_note: Concurrent competence is a constitutional allocation of lawmaking authority between governmental levels, a specific example of the powers and structure a constitution defines.
relation_locator: Basic Law Articles 70–72; Introduction to Political Science 1.1, constitutional structure

label: Standing to sue
card: In US federal court, standing ordinarily requires a concrete, particularized injury that is actual or imminent, linked to the challenged conduct and likely to be redressed by a favorable decision. Disagreeing with a policy is therefore different from showing the personal stake needed to bring the lawsuit.
claim_review: Cornell's federal-standing section gives injury, causation and likely redressability; the jurisdiction is explicit and ordinarily avoids implying this short statement exhausts every standing doctrine.
relation_note: Standing concerns a party's ability to bring suit; amicus participation lets a nonparty offer a brief under court rules. The comparison separates initiating litigation from contributing to its consideration.
relation_locator: Standing, Federal Court and Lujan test; Amicus curiae, opening and court rules

label: Amicus curiae
card: An amicus curiae is a nonparty who offers a court arguments or information through a brief. Having an interest in a case does not make the contributor a litigant. Participation follows the court's applicable rules, which govern when and how such outside submissions may be made.
claim_review: Cornell defines nonparty participation and identifies Supreme Court Rule 37 and appellate Rule 29; the card avoids an absolute permission requirement because procedures differ by court and filing context.
relation_note: Compare a nonparty's rule-governed contribution with the injury-based requirements for a plaintiff's federal standing. An amicus brief does not itself give its author party status.
relation_locator: Amicus curiae, definition and governing rules; Standing, federal test

label: Rule of lenity
card: The rule of lenity favors the defendant when a criminal statute remains ambiguous. It concerns interpreting the reach of a penal law, rather than deciding whether evidence proves the alleged conduct. Its rationale includes reserving the definition of crimes and punishments to lawmakers instead of judicial expansion.
claim_review: Cornell's definition and separation-of-powers rationale support criminal-law ambiguity and legislative responsibility; remains ambiguous avoids suggesting every initial uncertainty immediately triggers the rule.
relation_note: Lenity concerns ambiguity in a criminal law's meaning; the prosecution's burden concerns evidentiary proof of guilt. The sources support this distinction without treating them as interchangeable safeguards.
relation_locator: Rule of lenity, definition and rationale; Burden of proof, criminal standard

label: Habeas corpus
card: Habeas corpus brings the legality of custody before a court. In US federal practice, a detainee's petition is a civil action challenging detention rather than an ordinary new criminal trial. It can protect against unlawful confinement, but jurisdictional and procedural requirements limit when relief is available.
claim_review: Cornell's overview and federal-procedure discussion support custody review, civil action and procedural limits; the card does not promise a merits hearing or release whenever a petition is filed.
relation_note: Gideon's unsuccessful state habeas petition supplies a concrete example of challenging detention through habeas before later Supreme Court review; it does not establish that every habeas claim succeeds.
relation_locator: Habeas corpus, overview; Gideon v. Wainwright, Facts, Florida Supreme Court petition

label: Stare decisis
card: Stare decisis directs courts to follow precedent, supporting consistent and predictable law. Vertical precedent comes from a higher court; horizontal precedent concerns a court's own earlier decisions. The doctrine allows some precedents to be overruled, so continuity is a strong consideration rather than an absolute prohibition on change.
claim_review: Cornell distinguishes horizontal and vertical operation and states that precedent is not an inexorable command; some precedents does not imply lower courts may disregard binding higher-court decisions at will.
relation_note: Cornell explicitly uses Brown's rejection of the separate-but-equal precedent as an example showing that stare decisis is not absolute.
relation_locator: Stare decisis, final paragraph and Brown example

label: Burden of proof
card: The burden of proof concerns who must establish a proposition and what standard their evidence must meet. In US criminal cases, the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; most civil claims use preponderance of evidence. Different proceedings therefore demand different levels of evidentiary persuasion.
claim_review: Cornell's criminal/civil examples, production/persuasion distinction and jurisdictional qualifications support the card; most civil claims preserves exceptions and the criminal claim is confined to proving guilt.
relation_note: Compare the standard governing proof with a procedure asking whether a material factual dispute requires trial. Summary judgment does not simply replace evidentiary burdens with a judge's preference.
relation_locator: Burden of proof, standards; Summary judgment, Rule 56 and non-movant evidence

label: Summary judgment
card: In US federal civil procedure, summary judgment can resolve a claim without trial when no genuine dispute of material fact remains and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. It does not authorize choosing between competing evidence that a reasonable factfinder could resolve differently.
claim_review: Cornell's Rule 56 section and favorable-to-nonmovant discussion support both conditions and the factual-dispute limitation; the card is explicitly federal and civil rather than a universal rule for all courts.
relation_note: Both may be considered before trial, but summary judgment adjudicates a claim or issue while a preliminary injunction supplies interim protection before final judgment.
relation_locator: Summary judgment, overview and Rule 56; Preliminary injunction, definition and Winter factors

label: Preliminary injunction
card: A preliminary injunction provides court-ordered protection before final judgment. In US federal practice, the cited test considers likely success, likely irreparable harm, competing hardships and the public interest. The question is whether interim relief is justified while the dispute remains unresolved, not whether the applicant has already won.
claim_review: Cornell's Winter factors and Rule 65 discussion support the four considerations and interim role; federal qualification avoids treating varying state procedures as identical.
relation_note: Contrast temporary relief pending resolution with an adjudication without trial when material facts do not require a factfinder; the procedures answer different questions despite possible pretrial timing.
relation_locator: Preliminary injunction, definition and Winter; Summary judgment, Rule 56

label: Claim preclusion
card: Claim preclusion generally prevents a party from relitigating a cause of action after a final judgment on its merits. A losing plaintiff cannot simply sue the same defendant again on that claim; a winning plaintiff likewise cannot start another suit just to obtain additional recovery.
claim_review: Cornell's res judicata overview and Bar and Merger examples support both losing and winning plaintiffs; generally avoids treating the brief account as an exhaustive jurisdiction-independent test.
relation_note: The res judicata entry expressly distinguishes claim preclusion from issue preclusion; the former concerns the cause of action, while the latter concerns a decided issue.
relation_locator: Res judicata, opening and Bar and Merger; Collateral estoppel, opening

label: Issue preclusion
card: Issue preclusion prevents relitigation of a factual or legal issue already validly, finally and necessarily decided in an earlier proceeding. It can matter even when the later lawsuit is a different claim. The focus is the resolved issue, rather than a wholesale repetition of the original action.
claim_review: Cornell's collateral-estoppel definition and civil-procedure discussion support final and necessary determination; can matter avoids promising automatic preclusion without the jurisdiction's additional requirements.
relation_note: The linked accounts distinguish preventing a repeated claim from preventing a repeated decision on an essential issue, while acknowledging varied uses of the term res judicata.
relation_locator: Collateral estoppel, opening and civil procedure; Res judicata, distinction paragraph

label: Citizens' assemblies
card: Citizens' assemblies bring selected members of the public together to learn, hear contrasting evidence and deliberate on a policy question. In Ireland's process, participants discuss in small groups and make recommendations. Those recommendations are advisory: elected institutions retain responsibility for deciding legislation and government policy.
claim_review: Ireland's official FAQ supports evidence, facilitated discussion and advisory recommendations; the card explicitly bounds decision authority to the Irish process rather than every citizens' assembly internationally.
relation_note: The FAQ directly explains stratified random recruitment as the method for forming an Irish assembly intended to broadly reflect the wider population.
relation_locator: Citizens' Assembly FAQ, how it works, recommendations and member selection

label: Stratified sortition for citizens’ assemblies
card: Ireland's citizens' assembly recruitment combines chance with demographic balancing. Randomly invited households may nominate an adult applicant; members are then selected using demographic information so the group broadly resembles society. The resulting mini-public is intended to be diverse, rather than simply comprising whoever volunteers first.
claim_review: The official FAQ's recruitment paragraphs describe random household invitations, one adult nominee and stratified selection among applicants; intended and broadly avoid claiming perfect representativeness or eliminating nonresponse effects.
relation_note: The source explicitly identifies stratified selection as the membership-recruitment procedure for Irish citizens' assemblies, connecting mechanism and deliberative body.
relation_locator: Citizens' Assembly FAQ, How are members selected?, invitation and stratification paragraphs

label: Regulatory sandbox
card: A regulatory sandbox permits supervised testing of an innovation within defined limits. The UK's Financial Conduct Authority typically uses small, time-limited trials with real consumers. Acceptance does not remove authorization requirements or exempt a firm from national law, distinguishing controlled experimentation from unrestricted permission to operate.
claim_review: FCA sections on offers, tests and tools support real consumers, scale/duration limits, authorization and inability to waive national law; the specific mechanics remain attributed to this regulator's program.
relation_note: Compare time-limited regulatory testing with automatic statutory expiry: both impose a time boundary, but a sandbox limits a trial while a sunset provision ends legal authority unless renewed.
relation_locator: FCA Regulatory Sandbox, tests and tools; Sunset law, definition

label: Freedom of Information Act (United States)
card: The US Freedom of Information Act lets people request existing federal agency records, subject to specified exemptions. It does not require an agency to create new records, conduct research or answer a questionnaire. The right therefore concerns access to recorded information rather than a general government research service.
claim_review: FOIA.gov's definition and What can I ask for? support agency-record scope, exemptions and no new-research obligation; people avoids incorrectly limiting requesters to US citizens.
relation_note: FOIA concerns access to agency records; the Sunshine Act concerns observation of covered agency meetings. Their comparison distinguishes two transparency mechanisms with different scopes and exceptions.
relation_locator: FOIA.gov FAQ, definition and records; 5 USC 552b(a)–(c)

label: FOIA segregability
card: FOIA segregability means an exempt passage does not necessarily justify withholding an entire record. Federal agencies must consider partial disclosure and release reasonably separable nonexempt portions after redaction. The practical question is what can still be disclosed without revealing the information protected by a valid exemption.
claim_review: 5 USC 552(a)(8)(A)(ii) and the final paragraph of (b) require reasonable segregation and partial release; reasonably and valid exemption preserve limits rather than promising every document has releasable fragments.
relation_note: The statute itself imposes partial-disclosure and segregation duties within FOIA, tying the mechanism directly to the federal records-access regime.
relation_locator: 5 USC 552(a)(8)(A)(ii) and final paragraph of 552(b)

label: Government in the Sunshine Act
card: The Government in the Sunshine Act generally opens meetings of covered federal collegial agencies to public observation. Its definition does not cover every government gathering. Specified exceptions permit closure of portions, with formal voting and disclosure procedures, so openness is a structured legal requirement rather than an unlimited rule.
claim_review: 5 USC 552b(a)–(d) defines covered collegial agencies, public observation, exceptions and recorded votes; covered and portions avoid universalizing coverage or suggesting every discussion must be public.
relation_note: Meeting observation under section 552b and access to records under FOIA address different forms of government transparency; neither mechanism is treated as an automatic substitute for the other.
relation_locator: 5 USC 552b(a)–(d); FOIA.gov FAQ, agency records

label: Sunset provision
card: A sunset provision makes a law, program or agency expire after a specified period unless renewed through the required legislative process. Instead of requiring a fresh decision to terminate it, the provision makes continuation depend on renewed approval. This changes the default when lawmakers take no action.
claim_review: Cornell's sunset-law definition and two-year program example support automatic expiry and renewal; required legislative process avoids assuming every sunset uses identical review procedures.
relation_note: A sunset changes the default duration of legal authority; a sandbox bounds a supervised test. Their shared time limit is useful to compare without equating the institutional mechanisms.
relation_locator: Sunset law, definition and example; FCA Regulatory Sandbox, time-limited tests

label: South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission
card: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission addressed abuses associated with apartheid through separate work on human-rights violations, reparations and rehabilitation, and amnesty. Its committee structure shows that truth-finding, assistance to victims and decisions about perpetrators' amnesty were related tasks, rather than one undifferentiated act of forgiveness.
claim_review: The official TRC introduction identifies the post-apartheid mandate and three committees; the card describes institutional tasks rather than claiming universal reconciliation or automatic forgiveness.
relation_target: Conditional amnesty in South Africa's TRC
relation_note: The official site identifies the Amnesty Committee as one of the Commission's three components, directly locating amnesty decisions within its wider mandate.
relation_locator: TRC official introduction and three-committee mandate

label: Conditional amnesty in South Africa's TRC
card: Amnesty before South Africa's TRC was conditional, not automatic for politically connected violence. In a 1997 decision, Henry Khanyile's application failed because the committee found he had withheld relevant facts. The case shows why political context did not remove the requirement for full disclosure.
claim_review: The TRC's 18 August 1997 statement quotes the committee's section 20(1)(c) nondisclosure finding; the card reports its decision without asserting that disclosure alone guaranteed amnesty or retrying guilt independently.
relation_target: South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission
relation_note: The statement is an actual Amnesty Committee decision within the TRC process and expressly applies its statutory full-disclosure condition.
relation_locator: Statement on Amnesty Decisions, 18 August 1997, Henry Mkheyi Khanyile section

label: Brown v. Board of Education
card: Brown v. Board of Education rejected state-imposed racial segregation in US public education under equal protection. The Court treated separate schooling as inherently unequal, rather than asking only whether physical facilities matched. The decision challenged a legal framework of separation, although implementing desegregation required further proceedings and resistance persisted.
claim_review: The US Courts educational account supports the public-education holding and later compliance/resistance discussion; state-imposed and public preserve constitutional scope without claiming immediate practical integration or a rule covering every private activity.
relation_note: Brown illustrates the possibility of departing from precedent: Cornell's stare decisis entry expressly connects it with rejection of Plessy's separate-but-equal rule, while the court account supplies the education holding.
relation_locator: Access to Education — Rule of Law, Brown and Cooper sections; Stare decisis, Brown example

label: Gideon v. Wainwright
card: Gideon v. Wainwright established the right to appointed counsel for indigent defendants in state felony trials. After Gideon was denied a lawyer, the Supreme Court held that the Sixth Amendment guarantee applies to states through the Fourteenth Amendment. The case concerns fair criminal proceedings, not universal publicly funded legal representation.
claim_review: US Courts Facts and Reasoning support Florida felony prosecution, indigence, denial and incorporation; the card confines its claim to state felony trials rather than all civil disputes or every minor offense.
relation_note: The case summary explicitly records Gideon's state habeas petition challenging his detention after the denial of counsel, before his later Supreme Court petition.
relation_locator: Gideon v. Wainwright, Facts, Florida Supreme Court habeas petition
